Claude Code 2.1.97 Deep Dive: 50+ Changes Fully Analyzed

Apr 9, 2026
Vibe Sparking

Release date: 2026-04-09 Changes: 50+

Version Overview

Section titled “Version Overview”

2.1.97 is a major maintenance and feature release containing approximately 50+ changes, covering new features, permission systems, MCP, session recovery, NO_FLICKER rendering, enterprise integration, and numerous reliability fixes. The overall signal is clear: this version isn’t about single-point innovation, but about polishing Claude Code’s core execution surface to be more stable and better suited for high-frequency real-world development usage.

I. New Features

Section titled “I. New Features”

1. Focus View Toggle (Ctrl+O) in NO_FLICKER Mode

Section titled “1. Focus View Toggle (Ctrl+O) in NO_FLICKER Mode”

Change Content

  • Added Focus View in NO_FLICKER mode
  • Display includes: user prompt, one-line summary of tool calls, edit diffstats, final response

Problem Background

  • NO_FLICKER mode solves the traditional terminal flickering problem, but introduces another issue: information hierarchy can become mixed in long sessions
  • Users often don’t want to see all raw tool outputs, but want to quickly understand “what I asked, what it did, how much was changed, what was the final answer”

Use Cases

  • Quick review after long refactoring tasks
  • Recapping an agent’s work process to colleagues
  • Reviewing results after numerous Bash, Read, Edit, Write tool calls
  • Need to quickly locate operation summaries for failed tasks

Example

  • User asks Claude to refactor auth module
  • Focus View only shows:
    • prompt: “Refactor auth to JWT middleware”
    • tool summary: Read 4 files, Edit 3 files, Bash npm test
    • diffstats: +84 -27
    • final response: “JWT middleware refactor completed, tests pass”

Notes

  • Only available in NO_FLICKER mode
  • Better suited for summary browsing, not for replacing full step-by-step debugging
  • If you need to see detailed shell output step by step, still return to full view

Historical Context

  • 2.1.89 introduced CLAUDE_CODE_NO_FLICKER=1
  • 2.1.90 to 2.1.97 continuously fixed multiple NO_FLICKER rendering, scrolling, copying, and shortcut issues
  • This addition of Focus View indicates NO_FLICKER is transitioning from “experimental rendering layer” to “usable workflow interface” stage

Competitor Comparison

  • Codex CLI
    • Typically more focused on raw streaming output
    • Lacks this hierarchical focus review view
  • Gemini CLI
    • Emphasizes structured output and extension ecosystem
    • Also lacks this session summary view oriented toward long coding sessions

Future Trend Prediction

  • More view toggles may appear later, such as diff-only, tools-only, errors-only
  • Claude Code may gradually evolve terminal sessions into a “navigable work record interface” rather than just a text stream

2. refreshInterval Status Line Setting

Section titled “2. refreshInterval Status Line Setting”

Change Content

  • Added refreshInterval status bar setting
  • Allows status bar commands to automatically rerun every N seconds

Problem Background

  • Previously, status bar was more like static information or low-frequency updates
  • For real-time changing information like current branch status, task queues, backend service health status, single render wasn’t enough

Use Cases

  • Real-time display of git branch, worktree, repo status
  • Real-time display of local dev server, test watcher, CI status
  • Display current machine status or session information during remote development

Example

  • Execute a status command every 5 seconds, showing:
    • Current branch
    • Current worktree
    • Whether background tests pass
    • Whether current directory has uncommitted changes

Notes

  • Too frequent refreshing increases performance overhead
  • Status bar commands should be lightweight to avoid causing lag
  • Be especially careful with heavy git/status commands in large monorepos

Historical Context

  • 2.1.94 added richer status/UI information management
  • 2.1.97 simultaneously added workspace.git_worktree, these two changes are clearly complementary

Competitor Comparison

  • Codex CLI status UI is relatively simple, lacking this obvious customizable status bar refresh mechanism
  • Gemini CLI has footer/UI improvements, but support for “custom status command timed refresh” isn’t as development-workflow oriented as Claude Code

Future Trend Prediction

  • Status bar may later support more dynamic contexts like token usage, agent count, task status, network status
  • Long-term may evolve into customizable development cockpit

3. workspace.git_worktree Injected into Status Bar JSON

Section titled “3. workspace.git_worktree Injected into Status Bar JSON”

Change Content

  • When current directory is in a linked git worktree, status bar JSON input adds workspace.git_worktree

Problem Background

  • Git worktree is high-frequency advanced development usage, especially suitable for parallel bug fixing, parallel feature development, parallel agent execution
  • Many tools only recognize repo root, not current worktree identity, leading to misleading status

Use Cases

  • Opening multiple worktrees in one repository for different branch tasks
  • One Claude main session + multiple subagents each bound to different worktrees
  • Quickly confirm through status bar that you’re not in main working directory but in some linked worktree

Example

  • Main repository at /repo
  • Current directory at /repo-feature-auth
  • Status bar can display worktree=feature-auth

Notes

  • Only has value in linked worktree scenarios
  • Custom status scripts need to handle empty field cases

Historical Context

  • 2.1.92 improved --resume to directly restore sessions from other worktrees in same repo
  • This version fixes subagent worktree isolation leaking to parent Bash tool
  • Indicates Claude Code is systematically completing worktree-first development experience

Competitor Comparison

  • Codex CLI worktree experience is currently more “you handle paths yourself”
  • Gemini CLI also lacks this explicit worktree status exposure capability

Future Trend Prediction

  • May later add branch, dirty state, ahead/behind, repo root identity fields
  • Worktree may become default isolation unit for multi-agent parallel programming

4. Added ● N running Indicator in /agents

Section titled “4. Added ● N running Indicator in /agents”

Change Content

  • In /agents list, when an agent type has active subagent instances, displays ● N running

Problem Background

  • Claude Code’s subagent/agent system is gradually strengthening, but observability has been a barrier
  • Users often don’t know which agents are running, whether they’re dead or busy

Use Cases

  • Multiple subagents concurrently executing code search, testing, documentation summarization
  • Checking if an agent type already has instances running to avoid duplicate launches
  • Debugging agent stuck issues

Example

  • In /agents output see:
    • code-research ● 2 running
    • refactor-helper ● 1 running
    • docs-agent

Notes

  • This is visibility enhancement, doesn’t mean agent orchestration logic itself changed
  • If agent instance state synchronization is delayed, may still need to combine with specific session judgment

Historical Context

  • 2.1.89 added named subagents to @ mention typeahead
  • 2.1.92 fixed tmux changes causing permanent subagent spawning failure
  • This version also fixes subagent cwd/worktree leakage

Competitor Comparison

  • Codex CLI current mainstream usage is still more single-agent oriented
  • Gemini CLI has rich extension ecosystem, but native multi-subagent interaction management isn’t as deep as Claude Code

Future Trend Prediction

  • May later add agent CPU/time/token visualization
  • May eventually form interactive panel similar to “job manager / task supervisor”

5. Cedar Policy File Syntax Highlighting

Section titled “5. Cedar Policy File Syntax Highlighting”

Change Content

  • Added syntax highlighting for .cedar and .cedarpolicy files

Problem Background

  • Cedar is increasingly important DSL in permission policy domain, especially growing in cloud permissions, fine-grained authorization, and policy-as-code
  • Lack of syntax highlighting significantly reduces readability

Use Cases

  • Enterprise permission policy debugging
  • Developing internal authorization systems
  • Analyzing Cedar-based access policies

Example

  • When writing Cedar rules for “whether user can access certain resource”, keyword, condition, entity reference highlighting helps reduce misreading

Notes

  • Only syntax highlighting, not policy validator
  • Doesn’t mean Claude Code itself starts natively executing Cedar permission models, but has signaling significance

Competitor Comparison

  • This item is more about editing experience enhancement, competitors may not particularly emphasize it

Future Trend Prediction

  • May indicate Claude Code values policy-as-code scenarios more
  • Combined with continuous permission system hardening, has flavor of evolving toward enterprise security development tools

II. Permission & Security Fixes

Section titled “II. Permission & Security Fixes”

6. Fixed --dangerously-skip-permissions Silent Downgrade Issue

Section titled “6. Fixed --dangerously-skip-permissions Silent Downgrade Issue”

Problem Background

  • This parameter, as the name suggests, is very dangerous, meaning skip permission restrictions
  • Previously, after approving one write operation to protected path, would be silently downgraded to accept-edits mode
  • Worst part: users didn’t know it changed

Why This is Serious Problem

  • In automated scripts or controlled CI, this “I thought still fully allowed, actually already semi-allowed” behavior creates unpredictability
  • Not transparent security-wise, unreliable engineering-wise

Use Cases

  • Unattended automatic environment modifications
  • Large-scale migrations in trusted local sandboxes

Notes

  • Even after fix, not recommended for daily use of this parameter
  • Only use when you completely trust environment, explicitly accept risks

Historical Context

  • 2.1.90 started continuously strengthening permission model
  • Multiple permission fixes this version indicate permission system moving from “usable” to “predictable and consistent”

Competitor Comparison

  • Codex CLI has clearer full-auto/semi-auto mode distinction, but usually more straightforward in explainability
  • Gemini CLI YOLO/accept-edits is also clear
  • Claude Code fixing “mode semantic instability” problem is fundamentally crucial

7. Bash Tool Permission Hardening

Section titled “7. Bash Tool Permission Hardening”

Change Content

  • Strengthened env-var prefix checking
  • Strengthened network redirection related checking
  • Simultaneously reduced false positives for common commands

Problem Background

  • Bash permission control is difficult because shell syntax is too complex
  • Attacks or bypasses often hide in:
    • Environment variable prefixes
    • Wrapper commands
    • Redirections
    • Compound commands

Typical Problem Scenarios

  • FOO=bar curl ...
  • LANG=C rm foo
  • timeout 5 mkdir out
  • cmd > /sensitive/path

This Fix Value

  • On one hand plugging vulnerabilities, on other hand reducing false positives
  • Shows team isn’t just tightening, but balancing “high security + low friction”

Notes

  • Shell permission systems always have edge cases
  • High-risk environments should still rely on outer sandbox, not just trust CLI’s own rules

Historical Context

  • 2.1.89 fixed hook if condition failing to match env prefixes and compound commands
  • 2.1.90 strengthened PowerShell permission checking
  • 2.1.97 further improved Bash permission checking

Competitor Comparison

  • Codex CLI tends to use more outer isolation and mode control
  • Gemini CLI yolo/shell/accept-edits model easier to understand, but granularity may not be as high as Claude Code

Future Trend Prediction

  • May later introduce more formal shell command normalization layer
  • Long-term may develop into declarative command risk classification system

8. Permission Rule Name Colliding with JS Prototype Properties Causing settings.json to be Ignored

Section titled “8. Permission Rule Name Colliding with JS Prototype Properties Causing settings.json to be Ignored”

Problem Background

  • If permission rule name is JavaScript prototype property name like toString, settings.json would be silently ignored

Root Cause

  • Typical JS object key handling error
  • When using plain objects as maps, prototype pollution or prototype key collision is classic pitfall

Use Cases

  • When enterprises/teams define permission rule names themselves, accidentally hitting these reserved properties

Why Important

  • Worst part is “silent ignore”
  • Users think rules are effective, but entire permission configuration may not be effective

Notes

  • This type of problem exposes configuration system robustness was insufficient
  • For enterprise administrators, this silent failure is much more dangerous than explicit errors

Competitor Comparison

  • This is implementation layer quality issue, not feature comparison point
  • But from product maturity perspective, Claude Code is paying down this enterprise-level edge reliability debt

9. Managed-settings Allow Rules Still Effective After Removal Until Restart

Section titled “9. Managed-settings Allow Rules Still Effective After Removal Until Restart”

Problem Background

  • Administrator remotely removed allow rules, but old rules continued effective in local process until restart

Impact

  • Management policies cannot be immediately revoked
  • In security governance, this is serious consistency problem

Use Cases

  • Enterprise administrator urgently revoking access to certain directory, command, or network capability

Notes

  • Immediate effectiveness is very important for enterprises
  • Once this type of problem exists, significantly weakens managed settings credibility

Historical Context

  • 2.1.92 added forceRemoteSettingsRefresh, emphasizing fail-closed semantics
  • This version fixes hot update not revoking problem, belongs to same governance chain completion

10. permissions.additionalDirectories Mid-session Modifications Not Effective

Section titled “10. permissions.additionalDirectories Mid-session Modifications Not Effective”

Problem Background

  • Additional allowed directories in settings not applied when modified during session runtime

Scenario

  • Temporarily opening sibling repo, shared config directory, external script directory during development

Impact

  • Users modify configuration but still need to restart session, breaking flow

11. Error Removing --add-dir Permissions When Removing Directory from additionalDirectories

Section titled “11. Error Removing --add-dir Permissions When Removing Directory from additionalDirectories”

Problem Background

  • Directory exists both through settings and --add-dir
  • After removing from settings, should still retain access rights from --add-dir
  • Previously both were revoked together

Root Cause

  • Multi-source permission merging logic error
  • Didn’t correctly do source-aware permission bookkeeping

Why Important

  • Multi-layer permission sources is enterprise environment norm
  • Permission system must support “precise addition/removal by source”, cannot brutally override

III. MCP Related Fixes

Section titled “III. MCP Related Fixes”

12. MCP HTTP/SSE Reconnection Memory Leak, ~50MB/Hour

Section titled “12. MCP HTTP/SSE Reconnection Memory Leak, ~50MB/Hour”

Problem Background

  • MCP heavily relies on HTTP/SSE long connections
  • When server repeatedly reconnects, buffers not released
  • Long sessions or unstable network environments steadily consume memory

Use Cases

  • Long-term connections to databases, browsers, remote knowledge bases, internal tool MCP servers
  • Environments with average network quality where server actively disconnects and reconnects

Example

  • 8 hours workday, if leaking 50MB/hour, that’s 400MB
  • Combined with other caches and transcript, quickly becomes noticeable performance issue

Notes

  • This is typical stability pain point for “long-running agent tools”
  • Significantly impacts those using Claude Code as all-day development partner

Historical Context

  • 2.1.90 fixed SSE transport quadratic complexity issue for large streamed frames
  • 2.1.92 fixed plugin MCP stuck connecting
  • 2.1.97 fixes buffer unreleased, indicating MCP communication stack still being polished

Competitor Comparison

  • Codex CLI native MCP ecosystem not as heavy as Claude Code
  • Gemini CLI also pushing MCP/extensions, but Claude Code deeper in real IDE-like agent integration, so these problems exposed earlier

Future Trend Prediction

  • MCP will increasingly become “AI tool bus”
  • Stability, reconnection, backpressure, memory recycling will become next phase core engineering competition points

13. MCP OAuth oauth.authServerMetadataUrl Token Refresh Not Effective After Restart

Section titled “13. MCP OAuth oauth.authServerMetadataUrl Token Refresh Not Effective After Restart”

Problem Background

  • Enterprise identity providers like ADFS rely on this metadata URL
  • Token refresh after restart didn’t correctly honor this setting

Use Cases

  • Enterprise SSO login
  • Self-hosted OAuth or ADFS-compatible MCP services

Impact

  • Initial login may succeed, subsequent refreshes fail
  • Causes most annoying enterprise problem: “seems usable, suddenly breaks after some time”

Notes

  • These problems typically only appear heavily in enterprise environments, high compliance environments
  • Ordinary individual users may not encounter, but once encountered almost judged as unusable

IV. Rate Limit & API Reliability

Section titled “IV. Rate Limit & API Reliability”

14. Fixed 429 Retry Too Fast Exhaustion Problem

Section titled “14. Fixed 429 Retry Too Fast Exhaustion Problem”

Problem Background

  • Server returns small Retry-After
  • Client uses this small value as primary basis, causing too fast retries
  • All retries exhausted in about 13 seconds

Why This is Bad Experience

  • Users encounter recoverable rate limiting, but due to overly aggressive client strategy, directly becomes failure
  • Makes people mistakenly think “service completely unavailable”

Fix Content

  • Exponential backoff now applied as minimum lower bound
  • Even if server gives small Retry-After, won’t blindly densely retry

Use Cases

  • API temporary congestion
  • Enterprise proxy layer, Cloudflare, gateway layer rate limiting
  • High concurrency subagents triggering burst

Historical Context

  • 2.1.90 fixed rate-limit options dialog infinite loop
  • 2.1.94 fixed 429 long Retry-After causing appearance of hanging
  • 2.1.97 fixes small Retry-AAfter retry exhaustion problem

Historical Context

  • 2.1.90 fixed rate-limit options dialog infinite loop
  • 2.1.94 fixed 429 long Retry-After causing appearance of hanging
  • 2.1.97 fixes small Retry-After retry too fast

Competitor Comparison

  • All three tools encounter rate limiting
  • Claude Code has many fix records in this area, indicating they’re fine-tuning strategies at more granular level for real production traffic

Future Trend Prediction

  • May later add smarter per-model, per-endpoint, per-plan retry strategies
  • May also deeper integrate with UI, clearly telling users “I’m backing off and retrying, not stuck”

15. Context Compaction Causing Rate-limit Upgrade Options to Disappear

Section titled “15. Context Compaction Causing Rate-limit Upgrade Options to Disappear”

Problem Background

  • After being rate limited, system may suggest upgrade options or alternatives
  • But after context compaction, these prompts disappeared

Root Cause

  • UI state and session state not uniformly persisted

Impact

  • Users handling limit issues, then prompts disappear themselves, breaking experience

V. /resume & Transcript Persistence Fixes

Section titled “V. /resume & Transcript Persistence Fixes”

This group is one of the most important areas in this version, because they directly relate to whether Claude Code can become a “long-term continuous work agent”.

16. Multiple /resume Picker Issues Fixed

Section titled “16. Multiple /resume Picker Issues Fixed”

Issues Involved

  • --resume <name> not editable after opening
  • Ctrl+A reload clears search
  • Empty list swallows navigation
  • task-status overwrites conversation summary
  • Cross-project stale data

Problem Background

  • Resume picker has evolved from simple list to actual session index interface
  • Once UI state, search state, session metadata synchronization isn’t done well, experience becomes fragile

Use Cases

  • Finding specific work among large history sessions
  • Switching sessions across projects
  • Need to quickly continue previous day’s tasks

Future Significance

  • If Claude Code wants to become daily main development environment, resume experience must be as reliable as “workbench recovery”, not “try luck whether can reconnect”

17. Edit Diffs for Files Larger Than 10KB Disappear in --resume

Section titled “17. Edit Diffs for Files Larger Than 10KB Disappear in --resume”

Problem Background

  • Large file edits not showing diff after resume

Impact

  • After recovery you know changes were made, but don’t know what changed
  • Especially bad for refactoring or generative modifications

Scenario

  • Modifying large config files, large TS files, large Markdown documents

18. --resume Cache Miss and Attachment Message Transcript Loss

Section titled “18. --resume Cache Miss and Attachment Message Transcript Loss”

Problem Background

  • Attachment messages not saved to transcript
  • Causing missing context blocks during resume

Use Cases

  • Users dragging images, screenshots, design drafts for Claude analysis
  • Resuming session after disconnection

Significance

  • Multimodal sessions cannot only store text, otherwise resume isn’t complete

19. Messages Input While Claude Working Not Persisted

Section titled “19. Messages Input While Claude Working Not Persisted”

Problem Background

  • User inputs additional messages while Claude is working
  • These inputs not saved to transcript

Impact

  • During session recovery, those critical supplementary instructions lost
  • May even cause users thinking they already said, but Claude completely unaware after recovery

This Type Problem Very Damaging to Trust

  • Because it’s not obvious error, but “quietly forgot what you said”

Historical Context

  • 2.1.86, 2.1.89, 2.1.91, 2.1.92, 2.1.90 all have resume/transcript related fixes
  • Indicates resume is Claude Code’s high-frequency complex weak point, also key construction direction

Future Trend Prediction

  • Later likely evolve toward more structured transcript, event logs, checkpoint recovery
  • May also add stronger “recovery consistency verification” mechanisms

VI. Hook, Subagent & Compaction Related

Section titled “VI. Hook, Subagent & Compaction Related”

20. Stop/SubagentStop Hooks Fail in Long Sessions, Error Messages Distorted

Section titled “20. Stop/SubagentStop Hooks Fail in Long Sessions, Error Messages Distorted”

Problem Background

  • Hook execution fails during long sessions
  • Simultaneously API errors incorrectly displayed as “JSON validation failed”

Impact

  • Users misled during troubleshooting
  • Real hook evaluator errors obscured

Use Cases

  • Advanced users relying on Stop hooks for auditing, statistics, auto-commit, post-processing

Notes

  • Stronger hook system, more important error message accuracy
  • Otherwise users have no way to judge whether schema problem, API problem, or executor problem

21. Worktree Isolation or cwd: Override Subagent Leaking Working Directory Back to Parent Bash

Section titled “21. Worktree Isolation or cwd: Override Subagent Leaking Working Directory Back to Parent Bash”

Problem Background

  • Subagent runs in isolated worktree or custom cwd
  • After completion, parent session Bash tool polluted to that directory

Impact

  • Parent session subsequent commands execute in wrong directory
  • Easily causes “why suddenly modifying wrong repo / running wrong tests / reading wrong files”

Why Serious

  • This is typical isolation failure
  • In multi-agent parallel systems, once isolation boundaries leak, behavior becomes very hard to explain

22. Prompt-too-long Retry Repeatedly Writing Multi-MB Subagent Transcript

Section titled “22. Prompt-too-long Retry Repeatedly Writing Multi-MB Subagent Transcript”

Problem Background

  • Context too long triggers compaction/retry
  • Subagent transcript repeatedly written as multiple large files

Impact

  • Wastes disk
  • Amplifies transcript volume
  • Increases resume and IO overhead

Significance

  • Indicates compaction and subagent transcript pipeline had duplicate side effects in long sessions

VII. Plugin System Fixes

Section titled “VII. Plugin System Fixes”

23. Git-based Marketplace Plugin Updates Misreport “Already at Latest Version”

Section titled “23. Git-based Marketplace Plugin Updates Misreport “Already at Latest Version””

Problem Background

  • Plugin from git repository
  • Remote already has new commits
  • Local update misreports already latest

Impact

  • Users think plugin has no new version
  • Actually stuck in old code, problem hard to troubleshoot

Use Cases

  • Internal private plugins
  • Plugins under development
  • Marketplace plugins relying on Git rather than fixed releases

24. Plugin Frontmatter Name Hitting YAML Boolean Keywords Causing Slash Command Picker Crash

Section titled “24. Plugin Frontmatter Name Hitting YAML Boolean Keywords Causing Slash Command Picker Crash”

Problem Background

  • YAML parses yes/no/on/off/true/false as boolean values
  • If plugin frontmatter name not properly handled, picker crashes

Example

Notes

  • For plugin authors, best to always explicitly add quotes
  • For platform, this input should be safely normalized, not crashing UI

VIII. NO_FLICKER Mode Fixes Summary

Section titled “VIII. NO_FLICKER Mode Fixes Summary”

This version has a whole series around NO_FLICKER, indicating although promising, past few versions indeed experiencing “from can run to can be main long-term use” growing pains.

25. Copying Newline URLs Inserting Spaces

Section titled “25. Copying Newline URLs Inserting Spaces”

26. Zellij Scroll Rendering Artifacts

Section titled “26. Zellij Scroll Rendering Artifacts”

27. Hovering MCP Tool Result Crash

Section titled “27. Hovering MCP Tool Result Crash”

28. API Retries Causing Stale Streaming State Memory Leak

Section titled “28. API Retries Causing Stale Streaming State Memory Leak”

29. Windows Terminal Mouse Wheel Scroll Too Slow

Section titled “29. Windows Terminal Mouse Wheel Scroll Too Slow”

30. Custom Status Bar Not Displaying When Terminal Height Less Than 24 Lines

Section titled “30. Custom Status Bar Not Displaying When Terminal Height Less Than 24 Lines”

31. Warp Shift+Enter and Alt/Cmd+Arrow Shortcuts Fail

Section titled “31. Warp Shift+Enter and Alt/Cmd+Arrow Shortcuts Fail”

32. Windows Korean/Japanese/Unicode Copy Garbled Text

Section titled “32. Windows Korean/Japanese/Unicode Copy Garbled Text”

Common Problem Background

  • NO_FLICKER involves terminal rendering, text layout, mouse interaction, copy behavior, scroll caching, platform compatibility
  • Once such system transitions from simple stdout to “complex terminal UI engine”, edge problems explode

Significance

  • These fixes aren’t minor tweaks, but completing production capability of entire new rendering architecture

Competitor Comparison

  • Codex CLI simpler, fewer such advanced UI problems, but also less terminal interaction capability
  • Gemini CLI also has terminal UI, but Claude Code information density higher in coding session scenarios, therefore rendering complexity also higher

Future Trend Prediction

  • I’m optimistic it will eventually become default mode
  • But before becoming default, likely continue several more compatibility fix rounds

IX. Platform & Cloud Integration Compatibility

Section titled “IX. Platform & Cloud Integration Compatibility”

33. Bedrock SigV4 Authentication Failure When Environment Variables Set to Empty String

Section titled “33. Bedrock SigV4 Authentication Failure When Environment Variables Set to Empty String”

Problem Background

  • GitHub Actions often maps unset input values to empty strings, not undefined
  • AWS_BEARER_TOKEN_BEDROCK or ANTHROPIC_BEDROCK_BASE_URL if empty string, previously caused SigV4 authentication failure

Use Cases

  • GitHub Actions
  • CI/CD pipelines
  • Calling Claude through Bedrock

Why Important

  • Typical “works locally, explodes in CI” pitfall
  • Directly impacts automated deployment and enterprise pipelines

Historical Context

  • 2.1.94 added Mantle support and continued expanding Bedrock paths
  • 2.1.96 just fixed Bedrock 403 Authorization header regression
  • 2.1.97 fixes another Bedrock authentication edge problem

Conclusion

  • Bedrock path recently clearly in rapid compatibility period
  • Enterprise AWS users worth closely watching subsequent versions

X. Improvements

Section titled “X. Improvements”

34. Accept Edits Auto-approves Safe Env Prefix or Wrapper Commands

Section titled “34. Accept Edits Auto-approves Safe Env Prefix or Wrapper Commands”

Change Content

  • Commands like LANG=C rm foo
  • timeout 5 mkdir out Now auto-approved in Accept Edits mode

Problem Background

  • These prefixes themselves don’t add risk, just changing locale, timeout control, or wrapper execution
  • Previously treated as more dangerous commands, causing unnecessary confirmations

Significance

  • Reduces friction
  • Makes permission system better understand real shell world

35. Auto Mode and Bypass-permissions Mode Auto-approves Sandbox Network Access Prompts

Section titled “35. Auto Mode and Bypass-permissions Mode Auto-approves Sandbox Network Access Prompts”

Background

  • Certain modes already higher automation
  • Still frequently prompting for sandbox network access appears disjointed

Significance

  • Mode semantics more consistent
  • Automated tasks less likely interrupted by redundant prompts

36. sandbox.network.allowMachLookup Effective on macOS

Section titled “36. sandbox.network.allowMachLookup Effective on macOS”

Background

  • Mach lookup is macOS-specific IPC mechanism
  • Very significant for sandbox boundaries

Scenario

  • Restricting child process access to system services, background daemons

Significance

  • Indicates macOS sandbox model support deeper

37. Image Processing Uniformly Compressed to Same Token Budget as Read Tool

Section titled “37. Image Processing Uniformly Compressed to Same Token Budget as Read Tool”

Background

  • Pasted images, attachment images, Read tool reading images previously had inconsistent budgets
  • Users might just change input method, consume more tokens

Significance

  • Multimodal input experience more consistent
  • Cost and context usage more predictable

Competitor Comparison

  • Gemini CLI multimodal also important direction, but here Claude Code clearly handling “token fairness for same image different input paths” problem, more detailed

38. CJK Period Punctuation Also Triggers Slash Command / @ Mention Completion

Section titled “38. CJK Period Punctuation Also Triggers Slash Command / @ Mention Completion”

Background

  • Chinese/Japanese users often input / or @ directly after full-width periods, commas
  • Previously required space, clearly English-centric assumption

Significance

  • Good internationalization improvement
  • Significant real experience improvement for Chinese/Japanese users

Example

  • 先看一下这个文件。/resume
  • 这个函数有问题。@src/auth.ts

39. Bridge Sessions Display Local Repo, Branch, CWD in claude.ai Cards

Section titled “39. Bridge Sessions Display Local Repo, Branch, CWD in claude.ai Cards”

Background

  • Bridge connects local sessions to web interface
  • Previously web unclear which local project this session connected to

Significance

  • Reduces multi-project confusion
  • When remotely viewing session, quickly confirm context identity

40. Footer Indicators Fixed on Mode-indicator Line

Section titled “40. Footer Indicators Fixed on Mode-indicator Line”

Background

  • Focus, notifications etc. indicators line wrapping disrupts layout

Significance

  • Minor fix, but helps visual stability for long-term terminal use

41. Context-low Warning Becomes Transient Footer Notification

Section titled “41. Context-low Warning Becomes Transient Footer Notification”

Background

  • Context insufficient reminder occupying line long-term creates continuous noise

Significance

  • More like real notification, not long-term polluting layout
  • Indicates team values “UI continuous readability” more

42. Transcript Volume Optimization: Skip Empty Hook Entries, Limit Pre-edit File Copies

Section titled “42. Transcript Volume Optimization: Skip Empty Hook Entries, Limit Pre-edit File Copies”

Background

  • Long session transcripts become very large
  • Hooks and pre-edit copies easily become inflation sources

Significance

  • Reduces disk and IO pressure
  • Paves way for /resume and long session stability

43. Transcript Accuracy Improvement: Record Final Token Usage Per Chunk

Section titled “43. Transcript Accuracy Improvement: Record Final Token Usage Per Chunk”

Background

  • Previously may have recorded streaming placeholder token usage, not accurate enough

Significance

  • Statistics more trustworthy
  • Later cost analysis, performance tracing, product optimization more valuable

44. Bash Tool OTEL Tracing Improvement, Child Processes Inherit W3C TRACEPARENT

Section titled “44. Bash Tool OTEL Tracing Improvement, Child Processes Inherit W3C TRACEPARENT”

Background

  • If tracing enabled, want bash child processes triggered by Claude also enter same trace chain

Use Cases

  • Enterprise observability platforms
  • Debugging complex automation chains
  • Researching agent execution latency

Significance

  • Very enterprise, very engineering
  • Indicates Claude Code not just local toy, but developing toward operable, auditable, observable platform

XI. Documentation & Skill Updates

Section titled “XI. Documentation & Skill Updates”

45. /claude-api Skill Updated, Covering Managed Agents

Section titled “45. /claude-api Skill Updated, Covering Managed Agents”

Background

  • Claude API no longer just single model calls, but increasingly agent management and enterprise orchestration capabilities

Significance

  • Documentation layer also catching up with product evolution
  • Managed Agents clear future direction signal

XII. Cross-version Context Summary

Section titled “XII. Cross-version Context Summary”

Looking at 2.1.89 to 2.1.97 together, this evolution mainline very clear:

Mainline 1: NO_FLICKER from Experimental to Mainstream

Section titled “Mainline 1: NO_FLICKER from Experimental to Mainstream”
  • 2.1.89 introduced
  • Afterwards continuously fixed scrolling, copying, rendering, shortcuts, memory leaks
  • 2.1.97 starting to add “workflow-level features” like Focus View

Mainline 2: Permission System from Static Rules to Enterprise Governance

Section titled “Mainline 2: Permission System from Static Rules to Enterprise Governance”
  • Bash/PowerShell continuous hardening
  • Managed settings refresh and revocation fixes
  • additionalDirectories multi-source merging fixes
  • worktree/cwd isolation fixes

Mainline 3: /resume and Transcript Becoming Real Production Capability

Section titled “Mainline 3: /resume and Transcript Becoming Real Production Capability”
  • Multiple versions fixing transcript chain breaks, cache misses, history loss, recovery UI problems
  • Indicates Claude Code values “long-cycle continuous collaboration” highly

Mainline 4: MCP & Enterprise Cloud Integration Entering Deep Waters

Section titled “Mainline 4: MCP & Enterprise Cloud Integration Entering Deep Waters”
  • SSE performance
  • Memory leaks
  • OAuth refresh
  • Bedrock / ADFS / managed settings
  • These aren’t problems toy users encounter first, but high-frequency enterprise use exposes

XIII. Higher-level Comparison with Codex, Gemini CLI

Section titled “XIII. Higher-level Comparison with Codex, Gemini CLI”

Claude Code Characteristics

Section titled “Claude Code Characteristics”
  • Values session continuity more
  • Values permission governance and enterprise compliance more
  • Values multi-agent, worktree, resume, hooks, MCP combination capabilities more
  • Terminal UI more complex, therefore also more prone to expose rendering detail problems

Codex CLI Characteristics

Section titled “Codex CLI Characteristics”
  • Iterates extremely fast
  • Usually lighter, more direct
  • In many scenarios more “command execution and code agent” simple experience
  • Emphasis on complex UI and long session history management not as strong as Claude Code

Gemini CLI Characteristics

Section titled “Gemini CLI Characteristics”
  • Extension ecosystem very active
  • MCP/Extensions, Cloud, IDE plugin, JSON output, prompt completion etc. capabilities advancing fast
  • More like open platform CLI
  • But in long-term transcript recovery, multi-layer permission governance, subagent/worktree engineering deep waters, Claude Code product trajectory clearer

XIV. Future Evolution Trend Predictions

Section titled “XIV. Future Evolution Trend Predictions”

1. NO_FLICKER Likely Gradually Default

Section titled “1. NO_FLICKER Likely Gradually Default”

Because it’s no longer just solving flickering, but carrying new interaction capabilities.

2. Resume / Transcript System Will Continue Refactoring

Section titled “2. Resume / Transcript System Will Continue Refactoring”

Too many fixes in this area, indicating current format and process still have structural debt.

3. Multi-agent + Worktree Will Become Claude Code’s Core Differentiation

Section titled “3. Multi-agent + Worktree Will Become Claude Code’s Core Differentiation”

This path resembles “AI programming operating system”.

4. Permission System May Continue Declarative or Even Policy Language

Section titled “4. Permission System May Continue Declarative or Even Policy Language”

Especially combined with Cedar highlighting, managed settings, enterprise governance needs, resembles moving toward policy-driven agent execution.

5. Enterprise Observability & Auditability Will Continue Strengthening

Section titled “5. Enterprise Observability & Auditability Will Continue Strengthening”

OTEL tracing, managed settings, Bedrock, ADFS, these are what enterprise customers truly care about.

Final Conclusion

Section titled “Final Conclusion”

Claude Code 2.1.97 isn’t a “flashy feature version”, but a version strengthening core workflows to be more trustworthy, stable, enterprise-grade.

One sentence summary:

It’s continuing to push Claude Code from “very useful AI coding tool” toward “sustainable, governable, recoverable, observable AI development workbench”.

For ordinary individual users, this version’s most direct perception will be:

  • NO_FLICKER smoother
  • Permission prompts more reasonable
  • /resume more reliable
  • Chinese/Japanese input more natural

For heavy users and enterprise users, this version’s truly important aspects:

  • Permission system more consistent
  • MCP more stable
  • Transcript more trustworthy
  • Worktree/subagent isolation safer
  • Observability and cloud integration more mature

Claude Code 2.1.91 Deep Dive: Breaking Down All 13 Changes

Apr 3, 2026
Vibe Sparking

Analysis date: 2026-04-03 Source: Claude Code CHANGELOG.md

Claude Code 2.1.91 looks like a small patch release on paper, but it carries a surprisingly strong signal. These 13 updates span five themes at once: MCP maturity, enterprise safety, session reliability, token efficiency, and developer experience.

This article walks through each change, the problem behind it, practical use cases, caveats, related changes in earlier versions, and how it compares with Codex CLI and Gemini CLI.

Why 2.1.91 matters more than it looks

Section titled “Why 2.1.91 matters more than it looks”

At first glance, this is just a short changelog. In reality, it reveals several clear product directions:

  1. MCP is moving from “works” to “scales.”
  2. Enterprise controls are getting stricter and more explicit.
  3. Session durability remains a major engineering battlefield.
  4. Token economics are now being optimized at the tool-protocol level.

Let’s go change by change.

1. MCP large-result persistence override

Section titled “1. MCP large-result persistence override”

Change: Claude Code now supports _meta["anthropic/maxResultSizeChars"], allowing an MCP server to request a higher result retention cap of up to 500K characters.

Background

Section titled “Background”

Claude Code has default truncation limits for MCP tool results, roughly around 25K characters, to avoid flooding the context window. That works fine for small outputs, but it becomes painful when an MCP tool returns something genuinely important and naturally large, such as a database schema, a repository index, or a large search result.

Before this release, MCP server authors had no direct way to say: “this result is large, but it is also important—please keep more of it.”

Practical scenarios

Section titled “Practical scenarios”
  • Database schema inspection: a Postgres MCP server returns the full schema for 200+ tables
  • Code search: a repository-wide search returns many relevant code blocks that should remain intact
  • Document retrieval: an MCP-based RAG server returns several long but highly relevant documents

Technical detail

Section titled “Technical detail”

The MCP server can return metadata like this:

This is an Anthropic-specific vendor extension, built on top of the MCP _meta extension mechanism.

Caveats

Section titled “Caveats”
  • The cap is still finite: 500K is the upper bound
  • Larger results consume more context and may trigger compaction sooner
  • MCP servers must opt in explicitly

Related changes in earlier versions

Section titled “Related changes in earlier versions”
VersionRelated change
2.1.84MCP tool descriptions capped at 2KB
2.1.86Better prompt cache hit rate by removing dynamic tool-description content
2.1.89Fixed MCP error truncation to only the first content block

Comparison

Section titled “Comparison”
ProductLarge MCP result handling
Claude CodeServer-side override via _meta, up to 500K
Codex CLINo MCP support; uses native function calling
Gemini CLISupports MCP-style extensions, but no equivalent server-side size override

Trend

Section titled “Trend”

This is the kind of capability that may eventually become standardized in MCP itself. For now, Anthropic is moving faster through vendor extensions.

2. disableSkillShellExecution for enterprise safety

Section titled “2. disableSkillShellExecution for enterprise safety”

Change: A new setting disables inline shell execution in skills, custom slash commands, and plugin commands.

Background

Section titled “Background”

Skills are powerful, but that power comes with risk. If a skill can execute shell inline, then an untrusted or poorly audited skill can become a serious safety problem in enterprise environments.

This release finally adds a clean master switch.

Practical scenarios

Section titled “Practical scenarios”
  • Enterprise IT policy: centrally disable shell execution in third-party skills
  • CI/CD environments: reduce execution surface area in automated runs
  • Compliance-heavy organizations: ensure that all execution paths remain explicit and auditable

Caveats

Section titled “Caveats”
  • This only blocks inline shell execution inside skills/commands/plugins
  • It does not disable ordinary user-requested Bash tool calls
  • Existing skills that depend on inline shell execution may stop working

Related changes

Section titled “Related changes”
VersionRelated change
2.1.83managed-settings.d/ for modular enterprise policy
2.1.85Org policy can block plugin installation
2.1.78CLAUDE_CODE_SUBPROCESS_ENV_SCRUB to remove credentials from subprocesses

Comparison

Section titled “Comparison”
ProductControl model
Claude CodeExplicit disableSkillShellExecution switch
Codex CLIPlugin sandbox model with explicit permissions
Gemini CLIFine-grained Policy Engine allowlisting

This is a strong signal that Claude Code is continuing its shift from a hacker-friendly terminal tool toward a more controlled enterprise execution surface.

3. Multi-line prompts in deep links

Section titled “3. Multi-line prompts in deep links”

Change: claude-cli://open?q= now accepts encoded newlines (%0A) in prompts.

Why this matters

Section titled “Why this matters”

This sounds tiny, but it actually matters a lot for integration. Once deep links can carry multi-line prompts, Claude Code becomes easier to embed inside IDEs, documentation, tutorials, browser tools, and automation workflows.

Example

Section titled “Example”

Related changes

Section titled “Related changes”
VersionRelated change
2.1.85Deep-link query length raised to 5,000 chars
2.1.84Deep links open in the preferred terminal
2.1.89Fixed claude-cli:// not opening on macOS
2.1.83Added disableDeepLinkRegistration

Comparison

Section titled “Comparison”

Deep-link support remains a distinctive Claude Code advantage. Neither Codex CLI nor Gemini CLI currently has a comparable CLI protocol ecosystem.

4. Plugins can ship executables in bin/

Section titled “4. Plugins can ship executables in bin/”

Change: Plugins can now include executables under bin/ and invoke them as bare commands from Bash.

What this unlocks

Section titled “What this unlocks”

This moves plugins closer to being real, self-contained tool bundles rather than just wrappers around prompts, hooks, or MCP declarations.

Practical scenarios

Section titled “Practical scenarios”
  • A custom linter bundled as bin/my-linter
  • A schema/code generator packaged with the plugin
  • A workflow plugin that ships specialized infra tools

Caveats

Section titled “Caveats”
  • Files under bin/ still need correct executable permissions
  • Existing permission policies still apply
  • 2.1.86 recently fixed marketplace-plugin permission issues on macOS/Linux

Comparison

Section titled “Comparison”
ProductPlugin executable model
Claude CodeNative bin/ support for bare-command invocation
Codex CLIPlugin system supports custom tools, but with a different model
Gemini CLIExtensions are generally MCP/npm oriented, not bin/ oriented

This is a meaningful step toward a more serious plugin ecosystem.

5. Fixed transcript-chain breaks on --resume

Section titled “5. Fixed transcript-chain breaks on --resume”

Change: Claude Code fixed cases where async transcript write failures could silently break conversation history during --resume.

Why this is dangerous

Section titled “Why this is dangerous”

This is the worst kind of bug in an agent system: not a loud crash, but a silent loss of history. Users believe a session has been restored, but the context chain is already broken.

Practical scenarios

Section titled “Practical scenarios”
  • Resuming a long coding session the next day and finding part of the context gone
  • Recovering deferred tools in SDK or CI flows with missing state
  • Containerized remote sessions losing transcript integrity after restarts

Why --resume keeps showing up in the changelog

Section titled “Why --resume keeps showing up in the changelog”

Because it sits at the intersection of several hard problems:

  • tool/result consistency
  • async persistence timing
  • large-session durability
  • old-transcript compatibility
  • remote container lifecycle issues

Related fixes across versions

Section titled “Related fixes across versions”
VersionRelated fix
2.1.90Prompt-cache miss on --resume
2.1.89Older-transcript crashes; -p --resume hangs
2.1.86Missing tool_result chain restoration
2.1.85SDK history loss on resume
2.1.83Remote-session history loss after restart
2.1.77Silent truncation of recent history

Comparison

Section titled “Comparison”
ProductSession recovery model
Claude CodeFull transcript-chain restore via --resume
Codex CLISimpler session-file restore
Gemini CLI30-day history plus /rewind

Claude Code’s system is more ambitious, but that also means more complexity and more repair work.

6. Fixed cmd+delete across modern terminals

Section titled “6. Fixed cmd+delete across modern terminals”

Change: cmd+delete now correctly deletes to the start of the line in iTerm2, kitty, WezTerm, Ghostty, and Windows Terminal.

This is not a glamorous fix, but it’s exactly the sort of thing power users feel every day.

Root cause

Section titled “Root cause”

Different terminals emit different escape sequences for the same shortcut. Claude Code had only covered part of that landscape.

Fallback

Section titled “Fallback”

Ctrl+U remains the reliable readline-style fallback.

Comparison

Section titled “Comparison”

All three products face terminal compatibility friction. Claude Code is doing an especially thorough job of adapting to newer terminals like Ghostty and kitty.

7. Fixed plan mode in remote sessions

Section titled “7. Fixed plan mode in remote sessions”

Change: Claude Code fixed plan mode losing track of its plan file in remote sessions after container restarts.

What was happening

Section titled “What was happening”

Once the plan file path was lost, two bad things followed:

  1. Editing the plan triggered unnecessary permission prompts
  2. The plan-approval modal showed up empty

Impacted environments

Section titled “Impacted environments”
  • Remote Control sessions
  • Dev Containers
  • cloud IDEs such as Codespaces/Gitpod-like environments

Comparison

Section titled “Comparison”
ProductPlan mode + remote
Claude CodeMature plan mode plus remote control, now more reliable
Codex CLINo equivalent plan mode
Gemini CLIPlan mode by default, but no comparable remote-session stack

This fix highlights that Claude Code is increasingly operating as a persistent cross-device work environment, not just a local CLI.

8. Fixed schema validation for permissions.defaultMode: "auto"

Section titled “8. Fixed schema validation for permissions.defaultMode: "auto"”

Change: JSON schema validation now correctly accepts permissions.defaultMode: "auto".

This is a “small but important” fix. Even if the setting worked at runtime, a schema mismatch damages trust:

  • editors show red squiggles
  • teams doubt the docs
  • config rollout becomes noisier than it should be

For enterprise deployment, schema correctness matters more than many teams realize.

9. Fixed Windows rollback-copy cleanup

Section titled “9. Fixed Windows rollback-copy cleanup”

Change: Windows version cleanup no longer deletes the rollback copy of the active version.

This is classic reliability plumbing. Nobody notices it when it works, but when rollback is needed, it becomes critical.

Claude Code’s Windows installation model is heavier than npm-only tools like Codex CLI or Gemini CLI, so this kind of fix matters more in its ecosystem.

10. /feedback now explains why it is unavailable

Section titled “10. /feedback now explains why it is unavailable”

Change: /feedback no longer simply disappears; it now explains why it cannot be used.

This is a very good UX improvement. “Unavailable with explanation” is much better than “seems to have vanished.” That matters especially for:

  • enterprise deployments
  • third-party provider setups
  • proxy and managed environments

This reduces the chance that users interpret an intentional limitation as a broken product.

11. Improved /claude-api skill guidance

Section titled “11. Improved /claude-api skill guidance”

Change: Anthropic expanded the built-in /claude-api guidance around agent design patterns, including tool-surface choices, context management, and caching strategy.

This looks like a docs tweak, but it actually matters a lot. The competitive edge in 2026 is no longer just model quality. It is increasingly about:

  • how many tools you expose
  • how you control context growth
  • how you use caching well
  • when to split or avoid subagents

Anthropic is effectively productizing its own operational experience into reusable guidance.

12. Faster stripAnsi on Bun

Section titled “12. Faster stripAnsi on Bun”

Change: Claude Code now routes ANSI stripping through native Bun.stripANSI when running on Bun.

This is the kind of high-frequency micro-optimization that compounds over time. Each call is small, but log-heavy workflows invoke this path constantly.

Practical scenarios

Section titled “Practical scenarios”
  • long build logs
  • package installs
  • test runs with large terminal output

Gemini CLI and Codex CLI still primarily follow Node.js-first paths, so this kind of Bun-specific optimization is a notable differentiator.

13. Shorter old_string anchors in the Edit tool

Section titled “13. Shorter old_string anchors in the Edit tool”

Change: The Edit tool now uses shorter old_string anchors while still preserving uniqueness, reducing output tokens.

This is one of the most revealing changes in the whole release.

Why it matters

Section titled “Why it matters”

It shows that Claude Code is now optimizing token costs at the tool protocol level, not just at the prompt or model level.

In agent systems, cost comes from more than inference:

  • verbose tool schemas
  • repetitive file context
  • long edit anchors
  • redundant tool I/O

Once a team starts optimizing anchor length, it means they are thinking in terms of “token compound interest” across thousands of repeated actions.

Related token-efficiency improvements

Comparison

Final take: the five signals of 2.1.91

Section titled “Final take: the five signals of 2.1.91”

If you zoom out, Claude Code 2.1.91 sends five clear signals:

Bottom line

Section titled “Bottom line”

Claude Code’s strongest advantage right now is not one flashy feature. It is systems engineering for agents.

MCP, permissions, transcript recovery, remote workflows, and token efficiency are all converging into something more durable: a developer operating system for long-running AI-assisted work, not just a terminal coding assistant.

Claude Code 2.1.85 Deep Dive: Feature-by-Feature Analysis, Cross-Product Comparison & Evolution Trends

Mar 27, 2026
Vibe Sparking

Release Overview

Section titled “Release Overview”

2.1.85 is a “platform maturity” release — 9 new features + 17 bug fixes + 4 performance optimizations — centered on four themes: MCP ecosystem standardization, enterprise-grade hooks, terminal experience polish, and large-session stability.

New Features: Feature-by-Feature Analysis

Section titled “New Features: Feature-by-Feature Analysis”

1. MCP Multi-Server Environment Variables (CLAUDE_CODE_MCP_SERVER_NAME / CLAUDE_CODE_MCP_SERVER_URL)

Section titled “1. MCP Multi-Server Environment Variables (CLAUDE_CODE_MCP_SERVER_NAME / CLAUDE_CODE_MCP_SERVER_URL)”

Background: Previously, an MCP header helper script could only be hard-coded to serve one specific MCP server. If you had five MCP servers, you needed five nearly identical helper scripts.

Use cases:

  • An enterprise runs jira-mcp, confluence-mcp, and sentry-mcp — all of which need an OAuth Bearer token header injected in the same format
  • You can now write a single generic helper: #!/bin/bash echo "Authorization: Bearer $(get_token $CLAUDE_CODE_MCP_SERVER_NAME)"
  • At runtime, Claude Code automatically injects the current server’s name and URL

Notes: The helper script must be able to return different tokens dynamically based on server name/URL. Do not use a globally fixed value.

Cross-product comparison:

ProductMCP Header Customization
Claude CodeEnvironment variable injection — one helper serves multiple servers
Codex CLINo MCP support (OpenAI uses its own plugin system)
Gemini CLISupports MCP, but header customization is less granular than Claude Code

Trend: MCP header customization exists to accommodate enterprise authentication gateways and zero-trust network architectures. This may eventually evolve into declarative auth config (similar to Kubernetes ServiceAccount token auto-mounting).

2. Conditional Hook Execution (if Field with Permission-Rule Syntax)

Section titled “2. Conditional Hook Execution (if Field with Permission-Rule Syntax)”

Background: The previous hook system fired on everything — every PreToolUse event would fork a process to run the hook script, even if that hook only cared about git commands. Frequent process forking means added latency and wasted CPU.

Use case:

This triggers only when a git-related Bash command is executed; all other Bash calls (npm, python, etc.) are skipped outright.

Notes:

  • The if syntax reuses the permission-rule pattern-matching format (Bash(git *) means: the Bash tool, with arguments matching git *)
  • Non-matching hooks spawn no processes at all — it’s a pure string-match skip
  • Be careful with wildcard scope: Bash(rm *) will match rm -rf /

Cross-product comparison:

ProductHook Conditional Filtering
Claude Codeif condition using permission-rule syntax
Codex CLIHas a hook system but no conditional filtering; uses layered sandbox policies instead
Gemini CLINo hook system; uses coarse-grained tool policies

Trend: The hook system is evolving toward a “lightweight policy engine.” The progression goes: conditional matching → condition chains → a full declarative policy engine akin to OPA/Rego.

3. Scheduled Task Timestamp Markers (/loop and CronCreate transcript labels)

Section titled “3. Scheduled Task Timestamp Markers (/loop and CronCreate transcript labels)”

Background: When running tasks via /loop or cron, the transcript contained no record of when each execution was triggered. After the fact, there was no way to distinguish manual from automated triggers or reconstruct the timeline.

Use case:

  • You configure /loop to check CI status every 10 minutes
  • The transcript now shows entries like [2026-03-27 14:30:00 UTC — /loop triggered]
  • When reviewing a session, it’s immediately clear which actions were automated

Notes: Timestamps are in UTC. You’ll need to convert to local time manually.

Cross-product comparison:

ProductScheduled Task Auditability
Claude CodeInline timestamps embedded in the transcript
Codex CLINo built-in loop/cron mechanism
Gemini CLITask tracker was just integrated into the system prompt; no time markers yet

Trend: Auditability for AI agents is a hard requirement in enterprise procurement. This will likely evolve into OpenTelemetry span-level tracing.

4. Trailing Space After Pasted Image Placeholders ([Image #N] followed by a space)

Section titled “4. Trailing Space After Pasted Image Placeholders ([Image #N] followed by a space)”

Background: After pasting an image, the [Image #1] placeholder was immediately followed by user-typed text, causing the tokenizer to potentially merge the placeholder and the text.

Use case: After pasting a screenshot and typing “fix this CSS,” the result used to be [Image #1]fix this CSS. It now correctly produces [Image #1] fix this CSS.

Notes: A minor change, but important for the robustness of multimodal interactions.

Cross-product comparison: All three products support image pasting in similar ways. This is a polish-level detail that does not represent a competitive differentiator.

5. Deep Link Length Extended to 5,000 Characters

Section titled “5. Deep Link Length Extended to 5,000 Characters”

Background: The claude-cli://open?q=... deep link had a short character limit that prevented passing complex pre-filled prompts. CI/CD tools and IDE plugins wanting to open Claude Code with full context would have their payloads truncated.

Use cases:

  • A CI pipeline failure automatically generates a deep link: claude-cli://open?q=This%20build%20failed%20with%20error... (with the full error log attached)
  • Internal team wikis embed one-click debug links
  • Prompts that exceed a readable length display a “scroll to review” warning to prevent blind execution

Notes: The 5,000-character limit applies to the URL-encoded string; the actual content is shorter. Browsers also impose their own limits on total URL length.

Cross-product comparison:

ProductDeep Link / URL Scheme
Claude Codeclaude-cli://open?q=..., up to 5,000 characters
Codex CLINo standard deep link scheme
Gemini CLINo standard deep link scheme

Trend: Deep links are the bridge for IDE-to-CLI integration. A standardized coding agent URL scheme protocol is a likely future development.

6. MCP OAuth RFC 9728 Compliance

Section titled “6. MCP OAuth RFC 9728 Compliance”

Background: MCP OAuth previously used a custom discovery mechanism to locate the authorization server. RFC 9728 (Protected Resource Metadata), which became a standard in late 2024, defines how a resource server can advertise its associated authorization server for automatic discovery.

Use case:

  • The MCP server returns WWW-Authenticate: Bearer plus a resource_metadata URL
  • Claude Code automatically fetches that URL to retrieve authorization_server information
  • Users no longer need to manually configure the OAuth issuer, token endpoint, or other parameters

Notes:

  • The MCP server must also implement the RFC 9728 metadata endpoint
  • There may be transitional compatibility issues with the older discovery mechanism

Cross-product comparison:

ProductOAuth Standards Compliance
Claude CodeRFC 9728 discovery
Codex CLIN/A (does not use MCP OAuth)
Gemini CLIMCP support in progress; OAuth implementation details not yet public

Trend: MCP ecosystem authentication is converging from “every vendor rolling their own” toward RFC-standard flows. This is critical for enterprise SSO integration.

7. Organization Policy Blocks Plugin Installation (managed-settings.json)

Section titled “7. Organization Policy Blocks Plugin Installation (managed-settings.json)”

Background: Enterprise IT teams need control over which plugins can be installed. Previously, managed-settings.json could flag blocked plugins, but those plugins remained visible in the marketplace — users could see them but not install them, creating a confusing experience.

Use case: A company’s security policy prohibits all third-party shell-execution plugins. Those plugins now disappear entirely from the marketplace, so employees never encounter the confusing “why can’t I install this?” situation.

Notes: This is an organization-level setting and does not affect individual users. IT admins must maintain managed-settings.json.

Cross-product comparison:

ProductEnterprise Plugin Management
Claude Codemanaged-settings.json + marketplace hiding
Codex CLIProduct-scoped plugin sync just landed in v0.117
Gemini CLIHas a settings.json policy but no marketplace integration

Trend: All three vendors are accelerating enterprise control capabilities. The end state will likely align with MDM (Mobile Device Management)-level policy distribution.

8. PreToolUse Hook Satisfying AskUserQuestion (Headless Integration)

Section titled “8. PreToolUse Hook Satisfying AskUserQuestion (Headless Integration)”

Background: When Claude Code needs to ask the user a question (AskUserQuestion) in a headless or CI environment, there is no human available to respond. Previously, execution would simply time out and fail.

Use case:

The hook script returns {"permissionDecision": "allow", "updatedInput": "Yes, proceed with the refactor"}, automatically answering on behalf of the user.

This enables Claude Code to run fully unattended:

  • Automatically fixing lint issues in CI/CD
  • Batch refactoring tasks
  • Bridging user Q&A through a Slack bot

Notes:

  • Design the auto-answer logic carefully to avoid automatically saying “yes” when the agent is about to perform a dangerous operation
  • Pairing this with if conditional filtering is recommended so that only specific question types are auto-answered

Cross-product comparison:

ProductHeadless Auto-Response
Claude CodeHook returns updatedInput
Codex CLISupports --yes for global auto-approval, but without fine-grained control
Gemini CLINo comparable mechanism

Trend: This is a key piece of the “Agent-as-a-Service” puzzle. A complete Human-in-the-Loop API with routing to Slack/Teams/webhooks is a likely future development.

9. OTEL tool_parameters Gating (OTEL_LOG_TOOL_DETAILS=1)

Section titled “9. OTEL tool_parameters Gating (OTEL_LOG_TOOL_DETAILS=1)”

Background: tool_result events in OpenTelemetry traces include tool parameters by default, which can expose sensitive information — API keys, file contents, and so on — to monitoring systems.

Use case:

  • Production environments default to off: tool parameters are not recorded in OTEL logs
  • When debugging, set OTEL_LOG_TOOL_DETAILS=1 to enable full parameter logging

Notes: The default behavior has changed. Previously, parameters were always logged. Now they are not logged by default. If your monitoring pipeline depends on this data, you must opt in explicitly.

Cross-product comparison:

ProductOTEL Privacy Control
Claude CodeEnvironment variable gating
Codex CLISupports OTEL but no fine-grained gating
Gemini CLINo OTEL integration yet

Trend: Observability and privacy compliance are two sides of the same coin. Field-level redaction standards for OTEL are a likely future development.

Bug Fixes: Fix-by-Fix Analysis

Section titled “Bug Fixes: Fix-by-Fix Analysis”

Fix 1: /compact Fails on Oversized Conversations (“context exceeded”)

Section titled “Fix 1: /compact Fails on Oversized Conversations (“context exceeded”)”

Background: The /compact command works by sending the conversation to the LLM for summarization. When the conversation has grown so large that even the compact request itself exceeds the context window, execution enters a deadlock — it’s too large and needs compacting, but the compact operation itself is also too large to run.

Resolution: Likely implemented as a segmented compression approach or a truncate-then-compact strategy.

Cross-product comparison: Codex’s compaction now runs in the background to reduce UI blocking (see performance comparison below). Gemini CLI has no equivalent feature.

Fixes 2–3: Plugin Enable/Disable Path Mismatch & Worktree Error in Non-Git Repositories

Section titled “Fixes 2–3: Plugin Enable/Disable Path Mismatch & Worktree Error in Non-Git Repositories”

Background:

  • When the declared plugin location (in settings) and the actual installation location differ, enable/disable operations cannot find the file
  • Using --worktree in a non-git directory caused an immediate crash before the WorktreeCreate hook could even run

Cross-product note: Codex v0.117 also recently fixed a plugin gating-related bug.

Fix 4: deniedMcpServers Not Blocking claude.ai MCP Servers

Section titled “Fix 4: deniedMcpServers Not Blocking claude.ai MCP Servers”

Background: The deniedMcpServers security setting only blocked MCP servers configured through the CLI, not those passed through from the claude.ai web interface. This was a security vulnerability — the enterprise-configured blocklist could be bypassed.

Cross-product note: This is a Claude Code-specific issue, as it is the only product that connects to both CLI and web MCP sources simultaneously.

Fix 5: switch_display Not Working in Multi-Monitor Setups

Section titled “Fix 5: switch_display Not Working in Multi-Monitor Setups”

Background: The Computer Use tool’s switch_display action was returning “not available” in multi-monitor environments. Multi-monitor configurations are common in enterprise settings where computer use automation is relevant.

Cross-product note: Codex and Gemini CLI do not have built-in computer use capabilities.

Fix 6: Crash When OTEL Exporter Is Set to none

Section titled “Fix 6: Crash When OTEL Exporter Is Set to none”

Background: Setting OTEL_LOGS_EXPORTER=none to disable log export caused the program to crash. This was a straightforward null-value handling bug.

Fix 7: Diff Syntax Highlighting Broken in Non-Native Builds

Section titled “Fix 7: Diff Syntax Highlighting Broken in Non-Native Builds”

Background: Non-native builds packaged via pkg/bun were missing the tree-sitter WASM bindings.

Fix 8: MCP Step-Up Authorization Failure (When a Refresh Token Is Present)

Section titled “Fix 8: MCP Step-Up Authorization Failure (When a Refresh Token Is Present)”

Background: OAuth includes a “step-up auth” scenario where the user is already logged in but the server requires elevated permissions (for example, accessing sensitive data requires MFA). The server returns 403 insufficient_scope. When a refresh token is already present locally, the code incorrectly attempted to refresh rather than re-authenticate.

Example: An MCP server requires scope: admin:write, but the local token only has scope: read. The server returns 403. Claude Code should prompt for re-authorization rather than looping with the old refresh token.

Trend: As MCP servers integrate with enterprise IAM systems, step-up auth scenarios will become increasingly common.

Fixes 9–10: Remote Session Memory Leak & Persistent ECONNRESET Errors

Section titled “Fixes 9–10: Remote Session Memory Leak & Persistent ECONNRESET Errors”

Background:

  • In remote sessions, when a streaming response was interrupted, the response buffer was not released, causing memory to grow indefinitely
  • The edge connection layer was repeatedly retrying the same broken TCP connection on instability; this has been changed so each retry uses a fresh TCP connection

Cross-product note: Codex v0.117 also fixed similar stability issues in remote multi-agent sessions.

Fixes 11–15: Terminal Interaction & Input Handling

Section titled “Fixes 11–15: Terminal Interaction & Input Handling”
BugDescription
Prompt queue getting stuckAfter a slash command, the prompt gets stuck in the queue and cannot be recalled with the up arrow
Python SDK MCP servers missingMCP servers of type:'sdk' were being filtered out at startup
Raw key sequences in SSH/VSCodeTerminal sequences were not parsed correctly, causing garbled output
Remote Control stuck at “Requires Action”Status not updated after permission was resolved
shift+enter intercepted by typeaheadAttempting to insert a newline gets swallowed by autocomplete suggestions

Fixes 16–17: Scrolling and Terminal Exit

Section titled “Fixes 16–17: Scrolling and Terminal Exit”
BugDescription
Flickering when scrolling up during streaming outputStale content bleeding into the visible area
Keyboard protocol not restored after exiting Ghostty/Kitty/WezTermAfter quitting Claude Code, Ctrl+C and Ctrl+D stop working

Kitty keyboard protocol issue in detail: The Kitty keyboard protocol is an enhanced keyboard mode for modern terminals. Claude Code enabled enhanced mode on entry but did not send the CSI ? u reset sequence on exit. This left the terminal in enhanced mode, causing all keyboard shortcuts to behave abnormally.

Cross-product note: Codex v0.117 also fixed a similar terminal state restoration bug (Shift+Left shortcut in tmux). This is a common problem for all terminal TUI applications.

Performance Optimizations

Section titled “Performance Optimizations”

1. @-mention File Autocomplete Performance (Large Repositories)

Section titled “1. @-mention File Autocomplete Performance (Large Repositories)”

Background: Typing @ to trigger file autocomplete in a monorepo with tens of thousands of files previously caused noticeable lag or timeouts.

Cross-product note: Codex v0.117 also made significant UI responsiveness improvements in the app-server TUI.

2. Improved Dangerous Command Detection for PowerShell

Section titled “2. Improved Dangerous Command Detection for PowerShell”

Background: The previous PowerShell command allowlist/blocklist was incomplete, allowing some obfuscated dangerous commands — such as iex, an alias for Invoke-Expression — to evade detection.

3. Large Transcript Scrolling Performance (yoga-layout replaced with pure TypeScript)

Section titled “3. Large Transcript Scrolling Performance (yoga-layout replaced with pure TypeScript)”

Background: The TUI was using the WASM build of yoga-layout (Facebook’s Flexbox engine) for layout computation. The WASM bridge introduces serialization overhead that becomes a bottleneck when transcript content is large. Replacing it with a pure TypeScript implementation eliminates the cross-language call overhead.

Cross-product note: Codex enabled app-server TUI by default in v0.117, using a fundamentally different performance architecture (client-server separation).

4. UI Blocking During Large-Session Compaction

Section titled “4. UI Blocking During Large-Session Compaction”

Background: Compaction (context compression) is a CPU-intensive operation. Running it on the main thread freezes the UI.

Three-Product Comprehensive Comparison

Section titled “Three-Product Comprehensive Comparison”
DimensionClaude Code 2.1.85Codex CLI v0.117Gemini CLI v0.34
Hook SystemConditional filtering + headless auto-responseBasic hooksNone
MCP SupportRFC 9728 OAuth + multi-server headersProprietary plugin systemBasic MCP
Plugin EcosystemMarketplace + enterprise managementFirst-class status just introducedNo marketplace
Multi-AgentPrimarily single-agentMulti-agent v2 (path-based addressing)Local subagent execution + tool isolation
Enterprise Controlsmanaged-settings + plugin blockingProduct-scoped policiessettings.json policy
ObservabilityOTEL + privacy gatingBasic OTELNo OTEL
Terminal CompatibilityNumerous terminal bugs fixed this releaseTerminal state restoration fixedTerminal compatibility average
Scheduled Tasks/loop + CronCreateNone built-inTask tracker just integrated
Deep Link5,000 charactersNoneNone
Architecture DirectionHook + MCP platformizationRust rewrite + app-server separationSubagent + A2A protocol

Future Evolution Trends

Section titled “Future Evolution Trends”

1. Standardization of Agent Collaboration Layer

Section titled “1. Standardization of Agent Collaboration Layer”
  • Codex already has multi-agent v2 (path-based addressing: /root/agent_a)
  • Gemini is pushing the A2A (Agent-to-Agent) protocol with agent acknowledgment
  • Claude Code is primarily single-agent for now, but the hook system and headless capabilities are laying the groundwork for agent orchestration
  • Prediction: All three vendors will converge on some form of A2A or MCP agent-layer interoperability standard within 2026

2. From CLI to Platform

Section titled “2. From CLI to Platform”
  • Codex’s app-server architecture (WebSocket + remote TUI) is already not a traditional CLI
  • Claude Code’s deep link and remote session features are also moving in a platform direction
  • Prediction: Terminal coding agents will ultimately evolve into headless coding services with multiple frontends (CLI / IDE / Web / API)

3. Accelerating Enterprise Security Compliance

Section titled “3. Accelerating Enterprise Security Compliance”
  • All three vendors are adding managed settings and policy engines
  • OTEL observability is becoming a standard enterprise requirement
  • Prediction: SOC 2 and FedRAMP compliance certifications will become competitive moats for coding agent products

4. Hook System → Policy Engine → Agent Guardrails

Section titled “4. Hook System → Policy Engine → Agent Guardrails”
  • The if condition in Claude Code hooks is just the beginning
  • Prediction: This will eventually evolve into declarative policies (similar to OPA) supporting complex condition chains, approval workflows, and automatic rollbacks

5. MCP Ecosystem Explosion

Section titled “5. MCP Ecosystem Explosion”
  • RFC 9728 compliance = enterprise SSO integration unblocked
  • Step-up auth fix = support for tiered permissions in enterprise IAM
  • Prediction: MCP becomes the “HTTP” of AI agents — a universal tool-calling protocol. Claude Code currently leads on compliance

In one sentence: Claude Code 2.1.85 is an “enterprise-grade polish” release — not chasing flashy new capabilities, but making existing capabilities genuinely production-ready in enterprise environments. By comparison, Codex is more aggressive in architectural reconstruction (Rust + app-server), while Gemini is more aggressive in multi-agent collaboration. All three are taking different paths toward the same destination: a headless, observable, policy-governed coding agent platform.
