macos-use: Give AI Agents Real Hands on macOS

Mar 22, 2026
Vibe Sparking

AI agents can write code, search the web, and manage files. What they can’t do is reach across your screen and actually use the apps you work in — Slack, Xcode, Finder, Terminal. That gap has existed not because desktop control is technically impossible, but because the obvious approach (screenshots + vision model) was always a workaround for a problem macOS already solved differently.

macos-use removes that wall.

What It Is

Section titled “What It Is”

macos-use is an MCP server written in Swift. It lets Claude — or any MCP-compatible model — control desktop applications through macOS Accessibility APIs.

Not screenshots. The accessibility tree.

Every UI element in every macOS app — buttons, text fields, menus, lists — is exposed through Accessibility APIs as structured, hierarchical data. VoiceOver has relied on this for decades. Automated testing tools use it. macos-use connects this tree directly to Claude via MCP.

Instead of analyzing a 1200×800 image and guessing coordinates, the AI reads: AXButton, label="Send", enabled=true. Unambiguous. Resolution-independent. No vision model required.

Six Tools, Full Control

Section titled “Six Tools, Full Control”
ToolWhat It Does
open_application_and_traverseLaunch any app by name, bundle ID, or path
click_and_traverseClick at coordinates, see what changed
type_and_traverseType text into any field
press_key_and_traverseKeyboard shortcuts with modifier support
scrollScroll in any direction
refresh_traversalRe-read current UI state

Every action returns a diff by default — added elements, removed elements, modified attributes. The agent knows exactly what its action produced. No guessing whether the click landed.

Here’s what a real session looks like:

Why Not Screenshots

Section titled “Why Not Screenshots”

The screenshot approach has three hard problems.

Token cost. A 1080p screenshot dropped into context is expensive. macos-use returns compact JSON file paths — UI trees are saved to /tmp/macos-use/, not dumped into the model’s context window.

Unreliability. Pixel-based recognition depends on display resolution, scaling, dark mode, font rendering. Change monitors or toggle Dark Mode and coordinates shift. The accessibility tree is structural data — none of that matters.

No semantics. In a screenshot, the AI guesses whether something is a button and what it does. The accessibility tree says: AXButton, label="Send", enabled=true. No inference required.

Installation

Section titled “Installation”

Option 1: npx (easiest)

Section titled “Option 1: npx (easiest)”

Add to your Claude Desktop config:

Or via Claude Code CLI:

First run builds the Swift binary automatically — takes a moment, fast after that.

Option 2: Build from Source

Section titled “Option 2: Build from Source”

Point your config at the compiled binary:

Prerequisites: Xcode and Swift toolchain.

Accessibility Permissions

Section titled “Accessibility Permissions”

On first run, macOS will prompt for Accessibility permission. Go to System Settings → Privacy & Security → Accessibility and add your terminal or Claude Desktop. Without it, the Accessibility APIs return nothing.

What You Can Do With It

Section titled “What You Can Do With It”

Automate repetitive desktop routines. Open your morning apps, arrange windows, log into tools, initialize your workspace — tell Claude once, it runs it.

Cross-app workflows. Copy content from Safari, open Notion, paste and tag it, switch back. Previously this meant recording a Keyboard Maestro workflow by hand. Now describe it in natural language.

Full-stack Claude Code sessions. Write code, have Claude Code simultaneously control Xcode to run a build, switch to Simulator to check the UI — code and interface in the same AI session.

Accessibility use cases. For users with limited mobility, AI-driven desktop control is a real productivity tool. The semantic tree approach is more reliable than screenshot-based alternatives.

Caveats

Section titled “Caveats”

Coordinates are window-relative. click_and_traverse x/y coordinates are relative to the target app’s window, not the screen. If the window moves, stored coordinates need to be recalculated.

Unstable during animations. The accessibility tree is a snapshot. If an app is mid-transition, refresh_traversal may need to wait for the animation to finish before the state is accurate.

macOS only. No Windows, no Linux. Swift + macOS Accessibility APIs are platform-bound.

Comparison

Section titled “Comparison”
macos-usePlaywright/SeleniumScreenshot + Vision
ScopeAny macOS appBrowsers onlyAnything (needs vision model)
Token costLow (JSON diff)Low (DOM)High (images)
ReliabilityHigh (semantic)High (DOM)Low (pixels)
Setup complexityMedium (needs Swift)LowLow
Cross-platformmacOS onlyAll platformsAll platforms

If your task is browser-only, Playwright is more mature and better documented. macos-use’s value is native desktop applications — the space Playwright doesn’t reach.

If any part of your workflow involves a macOS native app, it’s worth trying.

Claude Code 2.1.80: --channels Lets MCP Servers Push Messages Into Your Session

Mar 20, 2026
Vibe Sparking

Claude Code 2.1.80: —channels Lets MCP Servers Push Messages Into Your Session

Section titled “Claude Code 2.1.80: —channels Lets MCP Servers Push Messages Into Your Session”

A Claude Code session has always been a conversation: you talk, the agent responds. MCP servers extended that — the agent could call external tools. But information only flowed one way, outward. The agent asked questions; servers answered them.

2.1.80 opens the reverse channel. --channels (research preview) lets MCP servers push messages into your running session. The tool that could only speak when spoken to just learned to raise its hand.

At a glance

Section titled “At a glance”
AreaWhat changed
Channels--channels (research preview) lets MCP servers push messages into your session
Skillseffort frontmatter for skills and slash commands overrides model effort level
Statuslinerate_limits field in statusline scripts shows Claude.ai usage (5-hour and 7-day windows)
Pluginssource: 'settings' declares plugin entries inline in settings.json
Plugin tipsCLI tool usage detection added alongside file pattern matching
ResumeFixed --resume dropping parallel tool results — no more [Tool result missing]
VoiceFixed WebSocket failures from Cloudflare bot detection on non-browser TLS fingerprints
APIFixed 400 errors with fine-grained tool streaming through API proxies, Bedrock, Vertex
RemoteFixed /remote-control appearing where it can’t function (gateway/third-party providers)
SandboxFixed /sandbox tab switching not responding to Tab or arrow keys
UXFaster @ file autocomplete in large repos; improved /effort, /permissions navigation
Performance~80MB memory savings on startup in 250k-file repos
SettingsFixed managed settings not applied at startup when remote-settings.json was cached
PluginsSimplified plugin install tips to single /plugin install command

The channel opens both ways

Section titled “The channel opens both ways”

MCP has been a one-way street. Your agent calls a tool, the server responds. That’s it. If something happens on the server side — a CI build fails, a deployment completes, a test suite finishes — the server has no way to tell the agent. You have to ask.

--channels changes this. An MCP server can now push a message into your active session without waiting to be called. Think about what that enables:

A deployment monitor MCP server watching your staging environment. Your agent is writing code. The deploy fails. The server pushes “deploy failed: missing env var DATABASE_URL on staging” directly into the session. The agent sees it, checks the config, fixes it.

A test runner MCP server that pushes results as they complete. Your agent doesn’t have to poll. It gets notified.

A team communication MCP server that pushes relevant Slack messages or PR review comments into your coding session.

This is a research preview, meaning the API surface may change. But the direction is clear: MCP is becoming a bidirectional messaging layer, not just a tool-calling protocol.

Skills learn to set their own pace

Section titled “Skills learn to set their own pace”

effort frontmatter in skills and slash commands lets the skill author override the model’s effort level when the skill is invoked.

Before this, effort was a global setting. You’d set it high for complex work, low for quick tasks, and toggle back and forth. Now the skill decides. A code formatting command runs at minimal effort because it doesn’t need deep reasoning. An architecture review skill demands maximum effort because shortcuts produce bad analysis.

This is a small YAML field with outsized impact. Skill authors can now design for the right level of reasoning rather than hoping the user has their effort setting dialed correctly.

Rate limits, visible

Section titled “Rate limits, visible”

rate_limits is a new field available to statusline scripts. It exposes Claude.ai’s 5-hour and 7-day usage windows with used_percentage and resets_at.

If you’ve ever been surprised by hitting a rate limit mid-task, this is the fix. Your statusline can now show something like “73% of 5h limit used, resets in 2h”. No more guessing.

This only applies to Claude.ai billing. API users with their own keys have different limits.

Plugins, declared inline

Section titled “Plugins, declared inline”

source: 'settings' is a new plugin marketplace source that lets you declare plugin entries directly in settings.json. No registry lookup, no install step. Write the plugin definition in your settings file, it’s loaded.

For teams that distribute internal plugins, this simplifies distribution. Push the settings.json change, everyone gets the plugin.

Combined with CLI tool usage detection for plugin tips (alongside existing file pattern matching), the plugin discovery story is getting smarter. Claude Code can now suggest plugins based on what CLI tools you’re running, not just what files exist in your project.

The resume fix that matters more than it sounds

Section titled “The resume fix that matters more than it sounds”

--resume was dropping parallel tool results. If your previous session had parallel tool calls, resuming it would show [Tool result missing] placeholders instead of the actual results.

This is worse than it sounds. Parallel tool calls are common in complex sessions — the agent reads multiple files at once, runs tests in parallel, searches across directories simultaneously. Losing those results on resume meant the agent lost context about what it had already done. It would re-read files, re-run searches, or worse, make decisions based on incomplete information.

Fixed. All tool_use/tool_result pairs now restore correctly.

Voice mode and API fixes

Section titled “Voice mode and API fixes”

Voice mode WebSocket connections were failing because Cloudflare’s bot detection was rejecting non-browser TLS fingerprints. Claude Code’s WebSocket client doesn’t look like a browser, so Cloudflare flagged it. Fixed by adjusting the TLS fingerprint handling.

Fine-grained tool streaming was returning 400 errors when used through API proxies, Bedrock, or Vertex. If you’re running Claude Code through enterprise infrastructure, this was likely hitting you. Fixed.

/remote-control was appearing in the command list for gateway and third-party provider deployments where it can’t actually function. Removed from those contexts.

Performance: 80MB lighter on large repos

Section titled “Performance: 80MB lighter on large repos”

Startup memory usage dropped by approximately 80MB on repositories with around 250,000 files. That’s a meaningful reduction. On a machine with 16GB of RAM running multiple Claude Code instances across different repos, this gives back roughly half a gigabyte.

The @ file autocomplete in large git repositories is also more responsive now. In repos with tens of thousands of files, there was a noticeable delay when typing @ to reference a file. Reduced.

UI polish

Section titled “UI polish”

Several navigation and display improvements:

/effort now shows what “auto” currently resolves to, matching the status bar indicator. Before, selecting “auto” gave you no feedback about what effort level was actually being used.

/permissions gained proper Tab and arrow key navigation within lists. Combined with the Tab/arrow fix for /sandbox, keyboard-driven navigation is now consistent across settings panels.

The background tasks panel responds to left arrow to close from the list view.

Plugin install tips simplified from a two-step flow to a single /plugin install command.

The settings fix you didn’t know you needed

Section titled “The settings fix you didn’t know you needed”

Managed settings — enabledPlugins, permissions.defaultMode, and policy-set environment variables — weren’t being applied at startup when remote-settings.json was cached from a prior session. If your organization manages Claude Code settings centrally, this meant fresh sessions could start with stale configuration.

This is the kind of bug that’s hard to diagnose because it’s intermittent. It only happens when the cached settings are different from the current ones. Fixed.

What this release signals

Section titled “What this release signals”

--channels is a research preview, but research previews in Claude Code have a track record of becoming stable features within a few releases. The fact that it shipped means the underlying architecture is ready.

The pattern across 2.1.80 is Claude Code becoming infrastructure rather than just a tool. Channels make it a message bus. Effort frontmatter makes skills self-describing. Rate limit visibility makes it observable. Inline plugin declarations make it configurable without external dependencies.

Each of these alone is a nice improvement. Together, they’re building blocks for something that looks less like a CLI and more like a development platform.

Update with claude update. If you build MCP servers, --channels is worth experimenting with now. If you write skills, add effort frontmatter. If you’ve been flying blind on rate limits, configure your statusline.

Chrome DevTools MCP: Give Your AI Coding Agent Direct Browser Control

Mar 18, 2026
Vibe Sparking

When debugging frontend issues, your AI coding agent can read code, edit files, run tests. But it can’t see the page. Opening DevTools, copying console errors, describing layouts, running Lighthouse manually, pasting scores back — that’s still on you.

That wall is gone. The Chrome DevTools team shipped an official MCP server: chrome-devtools-mcp.

What It Does

Section titled “What It Does”

29 tools across 6 categories:

Input automation — click, drag, fill forms, type text, handle dialogs, upload files

Navigation — open pages, switch tabs, wait for elements, close pages

Emulation — simulate devices, resize viewports

Performance — record traces, analyze performance insights (powered by the Chrome DevTools performance panel), take memory snapshots

Network — list requests, inspect request details

Debugging — read console messages (with source-mapped stack traces), take screenshots, capture DOM snapshots, run Lighthouse audits, execute JavaScript

Also supported: Cline, Codex, Windsurf, Warp, Amp, Factory CLI, Copilot CLI, Kiro, Visual Studio, OpenCode, Qoder. If it speaks MCP, it’s covered.

Test Your Setup

Section titled “Test Your Setup”

Enter this prompt in your coding agent:

The agent should open Chrome, navigate to the URL, record a performance trace, and return the analysis. If that works, the setup is correct.

What It Feels Like in Practice

Section titled “What It Feels Like in Practice”

The old workflow:

  1. Write code
  2. Switch to browser to check the result
  3. Open DevTools
  4. Copy console errors
  5. Paste back to the AI agent
  6. Repeat several rounds

Now you can say directly:

  • “Check why this page loads slowly”
  • “Fill the signup form and take a screenshot”
  • “Find why this API call returns 404”
  • “Run a Lighthouse audit on the homepage”

The agent opens Chrome, performs the actions, analyzes the results, and responds — all in the same conversation. The middleman step is gone.

Connecting to an Existing Chrome Instance

Section titled “Connecting to an Existing Chrome Instance”

By default, the MCP server launches its own Chrome. But sometimes you need an existing browser — the app requires login state, or you’re in a sandboxed environment that can’t start a new Chrome process.

Auto-connect (Chrome 144+):

  1. In Chrome, open chrome://inspect/#remote-debugging to enable remote debugging
  2. Add --autoConnect to MCP config

Manual connection (debugging port):

Start Chrome with the debugging port open:

Point the MCP config to that port:

Note: the manual approach requires Chrome to use a non-default user data directory. This is Chrome’s security policy, not an MCP limitation.

Slim Mode

Section titled “Slim Mode”

For basic browser interaction only, add --slim. Exposes just 3 tools: navigation, script execution, screenshots. Faster startup, cleaner tool list.

Privacy and Data Collection

Section titled “Privacy and Data Collection”

Two default-on data collection behaviors to be aware of:

  1. Usage statistics — Google collects tool invocation success rates, latency, and environment info. Opt out: add --no-usage-statistics, or set the CHROME_DEVTOOLS_MCP_NO_USAGE_STATISTICS environment variable
  2. CrUX data — Performance tools may send trace URLs to Google’s CrUX API to fetch real-user experience data. Opt out: add --no-performance-crux

If the CI environment variable is set, usage statistics collection is automatically disabled.

  • Node.js v20.19 or newer maintenance LTS

Comparison with Similar Tools

Section titled “Comparison with Similar Tools”

Browser automation MCPs already exist — Playwright MCP, Puppeteer MCP. What sets chrome-devtools-mcp apart:

  • Official Google product, directly interfaces with the Chrome DevTools protocol
  • Performance analysis capabilities are unique — no other tool can do trace recording with DevTools-level performance insights
  • Full Chrome DevTools debugging power, including source-mapped console stack traces
  • Connects to existing Chrome instances, preserving login state
  • Android device debugging support

Playwright MCP is stronger for cross-browser test automation. The two can coexist; pick based on the scenario.

Opus 4.6 + 1M Context: The Real Power Is What You Don't Load

Mar 18, 2026
Vibe Sparking

Opus 4.6 + 1M Context: The Real Power Is What You Don’t Load

Section titled “Opus 4.6 + 1M Context: The Real Power Is What You Don’t Load”

I had 147 MCP tools loaded in my Claude Code session. My context window was half-eaten before I typed a single prompt.

The hidden cost of MCP tools

Section titled “The hidden cost of MCP tools”

If you use Claude Code with multiple MCP servers, you’ve been in this situation without knowing it. Each server dumps its full tool definitions into the context at startup — names, descriptions, parameter schemas, everything. One server consumes 2,000 to 5,000 tokens. With a dozen servers configured, that’s 30,000 to 50,000 tokens of overhead before you’ve even started working.

My setup included Chrome DevTools, Kubernetes, WeChat Official Account, Wenyan publishing, Context7, Exa search, Dart tooling, sequential-thinking, and more. All those tool schemas competing for space from the first prompt.

With Opus 4.6’s 1M context window, you’d think this doesn’t matter. For short tasks, it doesn’t. But for long coding sessions — the kind where you debug across files, run tests, iterate on designs, publish content — every token is attention. More schema noise means less focus on your actual code.

Deferred loading: tools as a menu

Section titled “Deferred loading: tools as a menu”

Then I noticed something in my session’s system prompt: <available-deferred-tools>. A list of 147 tool names. Just names. No schemas, no parameter definitions.

When I needed a specific tool, Claude called ToolSearch to fetch the full definition on demand. Load it, use it, move on.

The difference: ~50,000 tokens down to ~735 tokens. That’s a 98% reduction in tool-related context overhead.

Why this matters with 1M context

Section titled “Why this matters with 1M context”

You might think 50K tokens is nothing in a 1M window. Here’s why it matters anyway.

Context isn’t just storage capacity. It’s the model’s attention span. Research on long-context models consistently shows that information in the middle of very long contexts gets less attention than information at the beginning and end. Tool schemas sitting in the middle of your context are noise that the model processes on every turn.

Deferred loading removes that noise entirely until it’s needed. When you switch from writing blog posts to debugging a Chrome extension, the chrome-devtools schemas appear at the point in conversation where they’re relevant — near your current work, not buried thousands of tokens back.

A full-day test

Section titled “A full-day test”

I tested this during a session that crossed six domains:

DomainMCP ServerWhen tools loaded
Blog writingFile tools (built-in)Session start
WeChat publishingwenyan-mcpHour 2
Chrome debuggingchrome-devtoolsHour 3
Kubernetes managementkubernetes-mcp-serverHour 4
Documentation lookupcontext7Throughout
Web searchexaAs needed

In the old model, all six servers’ tool schemas would have competed for attention from minute one. With deferred loading, each domain’s tools materialized when the conversation naturally reached that work.

After 8 hours, Claude’s responses were still precise. The session didn’t degrade.

How to check your setup

Section titled “How to check your setup”

Deferred tool loading is handled by Claude Code’s tool infrastructure. If your MCP servers support it, you’ll see <available-deferred-tools> in your session context instead of full tool schemas.

Check your configured MCP servers:

If you’re running 5+ MCP servers and notice session quality degrading over time, deferred loading might already be improving things behind the scenes. If it’s not available for your setup, consider which servers you actually need active for each session.

The principle

Section titled “The principle”

In AI-assisted development, what you choose not to load is as important as what you load. The 1M context window is powerful, but it’s not infinite attention. Deferred MCP tool loading is the architectural decision that makes that power sustainable across real working sessions.

Context is attention. Spend it on what matters.

Quick reference

Section titled “Quick reference”
MetricWithout deferred loadingWith deferred loading
Tool context overhead~30,000-50,000 tokens~735 tokens
Reduction—~98%
Session degradationNoticeable after 2-3 hoursMinimal after 8+ hours
Max practical MCP servers5-8 before context pressure20+ without issues

Claude Code 2.1.76: MCP Servers Can Now Ask You Questions

Mar 15, 2026
Vibe Sparking

Claude Code 2.1.76: MCP Servers Can Now Ask You Questions

Section titled “Claude Code 2.1.76: MCP Servers Can Now Ask You Questions”

MCP servers used to be one-way tools. Claude Code called them, they returned data, the conversation moved on. Starting with 2.1.76, an MCP server can pause the flow and ask you for input. A form dialog appears mid-task — you fill in the fields, the server continues with your answer. The tool boundary just became a two-way conversation.

At a glance

Section titled “At a glance”
AreaWhat changed
MCP elicitationMCP servers can request structured input mid-task via interactive dialog (form fields or browser URL)
Elicitation hooksNew Elicitation and ElicitationResult hooks to intercept and override responses
Session naming-n / --name flag sets a display name for the session at startup
Worktree sparse pathsworktree.sparsePaths setting for claude --worktree in large monorepos — sparse-checkout only the directories you need
PostCompact hookNew hook that fires after compaction completes
/effortSlash command to set model effort level
Deferred toolsToolSearch-loaded tools no longer lose input schemas after compaction
Auto-compactionCircuit breaker stops retrying after 3 consecutive failures
Plan modeNo longer asks for re-approval after the plan was already accepted
Voice modeKeypresses no longer swallowed while permission dialog or plan editor is open
Remote ControlSessions survive idle reaps, rapid messages batch properly, stale work items handled
Background agentsKilling a background agent now preserves partial results in context
Worktree performanceReads git refs directly, skips redundant fetch when remote branch is available locally
Model fallbackNotifications always visible with human-friendly model names

MCP elicitation

Section titled “MCP elicitation”

This is the headline. Until now, MCP tool calls were strictly request-response: Claude Code sends a request, the server sends back data. If the server needed additional information from you — credentials, a configuration choice, a confirmation — it had no way to ask.

MCP elicitation changes that. An MCP server can now send an elicitation request during a tool call. Claude Code renders it as an interactive dialog: form fields for structured input, or a browser URL for OAuth-style flows. You respond, and the server continues with your answer.

Two new hooks accompany this:

  • Elicitation fires when an MCP server requests input, before the dialog is shown. You can inspect, modify, or auto-respond.
  • ElicitationResult fires after you respond, before the result is sent back to the server. You can override or log what’s being returned.

This matters because it turns MCP tools from passive data sources into interactive collaborators. A database tool can ask which schema to use. A deployment tool can request confirmation before applying changes. An auth tool can redirect you to a login page and wait for the token.

Deferred tools: schema loss after compaction

Section titled “Deferred tools: schema loss after compaction”

If you use ToolSearch to load tools on demand (deferred tools), their input schemas were silently dropped after conversation compaction. Array parameters and number parameters would be rejected with type errors. The tool appeared to work, then stopped working after compaction, with no obvious explanation.

The root cause: compaction serialized tool definitions without preserving their full schemas. The fix ensures schemas survive the round-trip.

If you’ve been hitting unexpected type errors on tools that worked earlier in a session, this was it.

Auto-compaction circuit breaker

Section titled “Auto-compaction circuit breaker”

Auto-compaction was retrying indefinitely after consecutive failures. If compaction failed three times in a row, it would keep trying, burning tokens and time. A circuit breaker now stops after 3 attempts.

Session naming

Section titled “Session naming”

The -n / --name <name> flag sets a display name for the session at startup. Useful for Remote Control setups where you’re managing multiple sessions and need to tell them apart. Previously, Remote Control sessions showed “Interactive session” as the title. Now they derive the title from your first prompt, or you can set it explicitly.

Worktree sparse paths

Section titled “Worktree sparse paths”

For large monorepos, claude --worktree used to check out the entire repository. The new worktree.sparsePaths setting lets you specify which directories to include via git sparse-checkout. Only the directories you list get checked out.

Worktree startup is also faster. The implementation now reads git refs directly and skips redundant git fetch when the remote branch is already available locally. Stale worktrees left behind after an interrupted parallel run are automatically cleaned up.

/effort command

Section titled “/effort command”

A new slash command to set the model effort level. Previously you could only configure this through settings.

PostCompact hook

Section titled “PostCompact hook”

A new hook that fires after compaction completes. If you have workflows that need to react to compaction — rebuilding context, refreshing tool state, logging — this gives you a clean trigger point.

Enterprise: session quality survey

Section titled “Enterprise: session quality survey”

Enterprise admins can configure a session quality survey via the feedbackSurveyRate setting to control the sample rate.

Voice mode fixes

Section titled “Voice mode fixes”

Two fixes for voice mode:

  • Keypresses were being swallowed while a permission dialog or plan editor was open. If you tried to type while voice mode had a dialog up, your input disappeared.
  • /voice was not working on Windows when installed via npm.

Also, /voice now shows your dictation language on enable and warns when your language setting isn’t supported for voice input.

Plan mode fix

Section titled “Plan mode fix”

Plan mode was asking for re-approval after the plan was already accepted. You’d approve a plan, and it would ask again. Fixed.

Context limit fix

Section titled “Context limit fix”

Invoking a skill with model: frontmatter on a 1M-context session would trigger a spurious “Context limit reached” error. The session had plenty of room, but the skill invocation miscalculated available capacity.

Adaptive thinking error

Section titled “Adaptive thinking error”

Using non-standard model strings triggered “adaptive thinking is not supported on this model” errors. The model string validation is now more flexible.

Bash permission matching

Section titled “Bash permission matching”

Bash(cmd:*) permission rules were not matching when a quoted argument contained #. The # character was being interpreted as a comment delimiter in the pattern, breaking the match.

Also, the “don’t ask again” option in the Bash permission dialog was showing the full raw command for pipes and compound commands instead of a readable summary.

MCP reconnect spinner

Section titled “MCP reconnect spinner”

The MCP reconnect spinner was persisting after successful reconnection. The spinner would keep spinning even though the connection was restored.

LSP plugin registration

Section titled “LSP plugin registration”

LSP plugins were not registering servers when the LSP Manager initialized before marketplaces were reconciled. A race condition during startup.

Clipboard in tmux over SSH

Section titled “Clipboard in tmux over SSH”

Clipboard copying in tmux over SSH was broken. The fix attempts both direct terminal write and tmux clipboard integration.

/export path display

Section titled “/export path display”

/export was showing only the filename instead of the full file path in the success message. Not helpful when you need to find the exported file.

Transcript scrolling

Section titled “Transcript scrolling”

The transcript was not auto-scrolling to new messages after selecting text. You’d select something, and the transcript would stop following new output.

Escape key on login screen

Section titled “Escape key on login screen”

The Escape key was not working to exit the login method selection screen.

Remote Control fixes

Section titled “Remote Control fixes”

Three separate issues:

  • Sessions were silently dying when the server reaped an idle environment.
  • Rapid messages were being queued one-at-a-time instead of batched, causing latency.
  • Stale work items were causing redelivery after JWT refresh.

Bridge session recovery

Section titled “Bridge session recovery”

Bridge sessions were failing to recover after extended WebSocket disconnects.

Slash command resolution

Section titled “Slash command resolution”

Slash commands were not found when typing the exact name of a soft-hidden command. Also, slash commands were showing “Unknown skill” in some cases.

Background agent improvement

Section titled “Background agent improvement”

Killing a background agent now preserves its partial results in the conversation context. Previously, killing a background agent discarded everything it had done.

Model fallback notifications

Section titled “Model fallback notifications”

Model fallback notifications were hidden behind verbose mode. Now they’re always visible, with human-friendly model names instead of raw model IDs.

Blockquote readability

Section titled “Blockquote readability”

Blockquotes on dark terminal themes were rendered as dim text, making them hard to read. Now they use italic text with a left bar.

VS Code fix

Section titled “VS Code fix”

Gitignore patterns containing commas were silently excluding entire filetypes from the @-mention file picker. A comma in a gitignore pattern was being split into multiple patterns, each excluding more than intended.

—plugin-dir change

Section titled “—plugin-dir change”

--plugin-dir now only accepts one path to support subcommands. Use repeated --plugin-dir flags for multiple directories.

What 2.1.76 signals

Section titled “What 2.1.76 signals”

The headline feature — MCP elicitation — is a real capability expansion. MCP tools can now participate in conversations, not just respond to queries. That changes what integrations can do.

Everything else is stabilization. Deferred tools, auto-compaction, plan mode, voice mode, Remote Control, bridge sessions — these are the seams between features shipped in the 2.1.70-2.1.74 wave. The fixes are targeted and specific, addressing problems that users hit in real workflows.

The combination says: ship one new capability, harden everything around it. That’s the right cadence for a tool people rely on daily.

Reference links

  • Claude Code Changelog
  • Claude Code Documentation
  • VS Code Extension

wechat-decrypt: Unlock Your Own WeChat 4.x Chat History

Mar 10, 2026
Vibe Sparking

wechat-decrypt: Unlock Your Own WeChat 4.x Chat History

Section titled “wechat-decrypt: Unlock Your Own WeChat 4.x Chat History”

Your WeChat stores years of conversations, photos, voice messages, and shared files. All of it sits on your hard drive in SQLCipher 4 databases. Encrypted with AES-256-CBC, protected by 256,000 rounds of PBKDF2 key derivation. Yours in name only.

wechat-decrypt is a Python tool that changes this. It extracts encryption keys from the running WeChat process, decrypts approximately 26 local databases, and optionally streams new messages through a web UI in real time.

How WeChat 4.x Encryption Works

Section titled “How WeChat 4.x Encryption Works”

WeChat 4.x uses SQLCipher 4 to encrypt all local databases. The encryption scheme:

  • Algorithm: AES-256-CBC + HMAC-SHA512
  • Key derivation: PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA512 with 256,000 iterations
  • Per-database: Each database has its own unique salt and encryption key

The WCDB wrapper (WeChat’s custom SQLite layer) caches derived keys in process memory as a hex string in the format x'<64hex_key><32hex_salt>'. This is where wechat-decrypt finds its way in.

What wechat-decrypt Does

Section titled “What wechat-decrypt Does”

The tool works in three phases.

Phase 1: Key Extraction. It scans the running WeChat process memory for the hex key pattern. Each candidate key is validated by checking its HMAC against database page 1. Valid keys are saved to all_keys.json.

Phase 2: Batch Decryption. Using the extracted keys, it decrypts all local databases. The decrypted output includes session summaries, full chat histories (split across multiple message_*.db files), contacts, media indices, emoticon mappings, favorites, and social network data.

Phase 3: Real-Time Monitoring (optional). A web UI at localhost:5678 streams new messages via Server-Sent Events with roughly 100ms latency. Images render inline, and the tool handles emoji, link cards, files, mini-programs, and location shares.

There is also an MCP server that lets Claude query your chat history, search messages, and retrieve contacts.

Platform Support

Section titled “Platform Support”
PlatformKey ExtractorRequirements
Windowsfind_all_keys_win.pyAdmin privileges, WeChat running
macOSC-based scanner (Mach VM APIs)Xcode tools, ad-hoc code signing
Linuxfind_all_keys_linux.pyRoot or CAP_SYS_PTRACE

Getting Started

Section titled “Getting Started”

Prerequisites

Section titled “Prerequisites”
  • Python 3.10 or later
  • WeChat 4.x running on the same machine
  • pip install pycryptodome
  • Administrator/root privileges (required for process memory access)

Quick Start

Section titled “Quick Start”

Windows:

Linux:

macOS: Requires building the C scanner with Xcode tools and ad-hoc signing WeChat.app before key extraction works.

On first run, the tool auto-detects the WeChat data directory and creates config.json. If your installation is non-standard, edit the config manually:

Starting the Web Monitor

Section titled “Starting the Web Monitor”

Open http://localhost:5678 in your browser. New messages appear as they arrive. The tool monitors SQLite WAL file modification times (WAL files are pre-allocated at 4MB and their size never changes) and validates frame salt values to skip stale data.

Image Decryption

Section titled “Image Decryption”

WeChat has gone through three image encryption formats:

FormatEraMethodKey Source
Legacy XORBefore ~2025-07Single-byte XORAuto-detected
V1Transition periodAES-ECB + XORFixed key: cfcd208495d565ef
V22025-08 onwardAES-128-ECB + XORExtracted from process memory

For V2 images, run find_image_key_monitor.py to continuously extract AES-128 keys while viewing images in WeChat.

Claude AI Integration via MCP

Section titled “Claude AI Integration via MCP”

The included mcp_server.py exposes your decrypted chat data to Claude through the Model Context Protocol. After extracting keys with main.py, Claude can search messages, query contacts, and browse chat history directly.

Practical Use Cases

Section titled “Practical Use Cases”

Personal backup. Export and archive years of conversations before switching devices or accounts.

Search across history. Find that restaurant recommendation someone sent you two years ago. The decrypted databases are standard SQLite, queryable with any tool.

Message loss detection. The tool cross-references session and message databases to detect hidden or missing messages that WeChat’s UI does not show.

Data analysis. Feed your chat history to local LLMs or analysis scripts. The MCP integration makes this straightforward with Claude.

Things to Watch Out For

Section titled “Things to Watch Out For”
  • WeChat must be running during key extraction. The keys exist only in process memory.
  • Updating WeChat may change memory layouts. Check the project repository for compatibility notes.
  • V2 image decryption requires actively viewing images in WeChat while the key monitor runs.
  • On macOS, you need to ad-hoc sign WeChat.app for the memory scanner to work. This is a one-time setup.
  • Admin/root privileges are non-negotiable. Process memory access requires elevated permissions on all platforms.

Legal and Ethical Use

Section titled “Legal and Ethical Use”

The project states clearly: use only for decrypting your own WeChat data, in compliance with applicable law. Do not use this tool to access other people’s accounts or data. This is a personal data recovery and backup tool.

Comparison with Alternatives

Section titled “Comparison with Alternatives”

Most WeChat backup tools work through the official backup/restore API, which limits you to transferring data between devices. wechat-decrypt operates at the database level, giving you raw access to the underlying SQLite files. This means:

  • Full-text search across all message history
  • Programmatic access via standard SQLite tools
  • Real-time streaming that the official tools do not offer
  • AI integration through MCP

The trade-off is complexity: you need Python, admin rights, and a running WeChat process. The official tools are simpler but less capable.

References

Section titled “References”
  • wechat-decrypt on GitHub
  • Usage Guide (USAGE.md)
  • SQLCipher Documentation
  • Model Context Protocol (MCP)

The Coding Agent Harness: Why Context Engineering Beats Model Shopping

Mar 4, 2026
Vibe Sparking

The Coding Agent Harness: Why Context Engineering Beats Model Shopping

Section titled “The Coding Agent Harness: Why Context Engineering Beats Model Shopping”

Your team adopted an AI coding agent last month. The first week felt electric. By week three, the pattern became clear: sometimes the agent nails it, sometimes it produces code that looks plausible but crumbles under review. Duplicate logic in three places. A helper function recreated from scratch when one already exists in utils. An N+1 query hiding inside a loop.

You start wondering if you picked the wrong model.

You didn’t. The model was never the problem.

The Insight Most Teams Miss

Section titled “The Insight Most Teams Miss”

Julian de Angelis at MercadoLibre has been deploying AI coding agents across nearly 20,000 developers and thousands of repositories. His conclusion after operating at that scale:

Your AI coding agent is a brilliant new hire on day one. Fast, eager, and with zero context about your codebase, your conventions, or your architecture.

You wouldn’t hand a new engineer a Jira ticket that says “fix this bug” and walk away. You’d onboard them: docs, tech stack overview, style guides, release workflows, access to internal tools, a mentor to review their work.

That onboarding system is what de Angelis calls the agent harness - the structured set of controls that shape what the agent knows, what it can do, and how its work gets validated. The underlying discipline is context engineering: designing and controlling everything an LLM sees before it generates a single token.

The Constraint Nobody Talks About

Section titled “The Constraint Nobody Talks About”

Every popular AI coding agent - Claude Code, Cursor, Codex - runs the same fundamental loop:

Read -> Plan -> Code -> Validate -> Iterate

The agent reads your files, plans an approach, writes code, runs tests, and loops back if something fails. At every iteration, the context window grows. System prompts, tool definitions, conversation history, file contents, terminal output, the agent’s own generated code - all of it accumulates in a finite workspace.

Here’s the part that surprises people: past roughly 60% utilization of the context window, more context makes the agent actively worse. This phenomenon is called context rot. Even with windows reaching 1M tokens, the fundamental challenge remains. Every token spent on a verbose tool result or an overly long rules file is a token not available for the actual task.

The best agent harnesses are designed with this reality at the center: inject the right context at the right moment, and avoid polluting the window with anything else.

Four Levers That Actually Matter

Section titled “Four Levers That Actually Matter”

1. Custom Rules

Section titled “1. Custom Rules”

Files like CLAUDE.md, cursor/rules, or AGENTS.md get injected into the agent’s context at the start of every interaction. This is the most accessible lever.

What goes in:

  • Tech stack and architecture patterns
  • Naming conventions and code style
  • Testing philosophy (“always write unit tests with table-driven inputs”)
  • Common pitfalls specific to your codebase
  • Anti-patterns you’ve seen the agent produce repeatedly

What doesn’t belong:

  • Entire API documentation (too long, wastes context)
  • Obvious instructions (“write clean code”)
  • Contradictory rules

Practical tips:

  • Keep them under 500 lines. Precision matters.
  • Split rules into focused files by concern: architecture, testing, code style, security. The agent loads only what’s relevant.
  • Include few-shot examples. Models learn from examples better than abstract instructions.
  • Make them living documents. Every time the agent makes a mistake, update the rules. Over weeks, this file becomes remarkably effective.

2. MCP Servers

Section titled “2. MCP Servers”

MCP (Model Context Protocol) servers are plugins that give the agent tools beyond reading and writing files. Without them, the agent is limited to what’s in the repo. With them, it can:

  • Query your database to understand schema and data
  • Search internal documentation or wikis
  • Look up API contracts
  • Interact with CI/CD pipelines
  • Access design specs from Figma
  • Validate its own output against real systems

MCP servers bridge the gap between the agent and your organization’s knowledge. They give the agent access to the same resources a human developer would use.

3. Skills

Section titled “3. Skills”

Skills give the agent new capabilities and domain expertise. A skill is a directory with an entrypoint file that can bundle templates, example outputs, reference docs, and executable scripts.

The design is clever: only a short description stays in context permanently, so the agent knows what’s available. The full content loads only when the skill is invoked - by the user or automatically when the agent detects relevance. This on-demand loading means skills can be as detailed as needed without permanently consuming context budget.

They come in two flavors:

  • Reference skills inject knowledge: conventions, patterns, domain context
  • Task skills provide step-by-step instructions for specific actions

The real power is that skills can bundle and execute scripts, run in isolated subagents with their own clean context window, and compose together. Programmable, context-aware, composable units of agent behavior.

4. Spec-Driven Development

Section titled “4. Spec-Driven Development”

This one reframes how you interact with agents entirely.

Consider this prompt: “Make a new feature to add new items from the backoffice.”

Seems simple. But it says nothing about: which tech stack, where the backoffice is, API contracts, storage layer, idempotency handling, authorization rules.

The agent will read the codebase, plan something reasonable, and produce a working MVP. You add an item and it works. You click “add” again and it inserts the item twice. It was “obvious” the agent should have managed idempotency by ID. In your business, it’s “obvious” that only one role can insert items.

The problem isn’t the agent. It’s the bare initial input. The bottleneck sits between the chair and the screen.

Spec-Driven Development (SDD) solves this by writing detailed specifications before the agent writes code. What the feature does, how it integrates, edge cases, acceptance criteria, test plans. The spec becomes the harness - it consolidates architecture decisions, guidance, and review criteria into a single artifact that engineers the agent’s entire context window in one shot.

And you can use the agent to write the specs too.

The Feedback Loop

Section titled “The Feedback Loop”

The four levers define what the agent knows and can do. The piece that makes the whole system converge is the feedback loop: tests, linters, type checkers, build scripts. Every tool that produces a pass/fail signal becomes a self-correction mechanism.

Agent hooks make this enforceable. They are user-defined commands that execute automatically at specific points in the agent’s lifecycle. Wire your validation into a Stop hook, and the agent literally cannot finish until the checks pass. Not a suggestion it might ignore. An enforced gate.

The more structured feedback available, the less human intervention is needed.

MercadoLibre’s Playbook at 20,000 Developers

Section titled “MercadoLibre’s Playbook at 20,000 Developers”

Theory is fine. Here’s what works at scale with 9+ technology stacks, thousands of legacy repositories, and multiple knowledge domains:

Standardized rules per technology. A curated set of custom rules at the org level, tuned to each tech stack, internal libraries, and code review standards. Teams inherit the base and layer on repo-specific rules. Getting the specificity right is critical - too specific breaks legacy projects, too loose lets unapproved libraries through (security risk).

Internal MCP servers. Built-in access to internal cloud platform capabilities, internal SDKs, business context via RAG, and updated application documentation.

Custom code review agents. Standalone review agents running in CI that analyze every PR - human-written or AI-generated - before a human reviewer sees it. They return prioritized findings so engineers see critical issues first. Human reviewers focus on design decisions instead of catching style violations. Faster review cycles, more consistent quality, and a safety net that scales with PR volume, not reviewer headcount.

Start Here

Section titled “Start Here”

If you haven’t built an agent harness yet, start with the simplest lever: custom rules. Create a CLAUDE.md or equivalent file with your coding conventions, common pitfalls, and a couple of concrete examples of good and bad patterns in your codebase.

Run it for a week. Every time the agent produces something wrong, add a rule. By the end of the month, that file will have quietly transformed your results more than any model upgrade could.

The teams that win with AI coding agents won’t be the ones using the fanciest model. They’ll be the ones with the best-engineered harness.

Based on Julian de Angelis’s analysis of AI coding agent deployment at MercadoLibre. Original thread.

Claude Agent SDK: From Weekend Hacks to Production-Ready Agents

Feb 2, 2026
Vibe Sparking

The Weekend That Changed Everything

Section titled “The Weekend That Changed Everything”

Nick Spisak spent a weekend pushing Claude Agent SDK to its limits. What started as casual experimentation turned into a deep dive through the SDK’s internals—and he came back with six patterns that separate toy demos from production-grade agents.

Here’s what he found.

1. Lifecycle Hooks: Your Agent’s Guardrails

Section titled “1. Lifecycle Hooks: Your Agent’s Guardrails”

The SDK exposes three hooks that let you intercept agent behavior:

  • PreToolUse — runs before any tool call. Perfect for validation, rate limiting, or blocking dangerous operations.
  • PostToolUse — runs after tool results return. Audit logs, result transformation, cost tracking.
  • Stop — graceful shutdown. Clean up resources, save state, close connections.

Without these hooks, you’re flying blind. With them, you control what your agent can actually do.

2. Skill Hot-Reload: Update Without Restart

Section titled “2. Skill Hot-Reload: Update Without Restart”

Agents accumulate context over long sessions. Killing them to deploy a fix means losing all that context.

The /reload-skills command solves this. One command reloads skill definitions from disk while keeping the session alive. No restart, no context loss.

I’ve used this to iterate on a skill five times in one debugging session. The agent kept its memory of what we’d tried before.

3. Session Teleportation: Move Your Agent

Section titled “3. Session Teleportation: Move Your Agent”

Sometimes you need to move a running session to another machine. Maybe you’re switching laptops. Maybe the session started on a server and you want it local.

/teleport session-id serializes the full session state—conversation history, tool states, everything—and reconstructs it elsewhere. The agent picks up exactly where it left off.

This works across machines. I’ve teleported sessions from my MacBook to a Linux server mid-conversation.

4. Dynamic MCP Loading: Solve Context Pollution

Section titled “4. Dynamic MCP Loading: Solve Context Pollution”

Here’s the problem: loading all 50 MCP servers at startup dumps thousands of tool descriptions into your context window. Most calls only use 2-3 tools. You’re paying tokens for tools you never touch.

The fix: ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH=true

Instead of loading everything upfront, the agent searches for relevant tools on demand. Nick measured an 85% reduction in token overhead with this approach.

The tradeoff? Slightly higher latency on first tool use while it searches. Worth it for most workloads.

5. Custom Agents: Automatic Delegation

Section titled “5. Custom Agents: Automatic Delegation”

Create specialized agents in .claude/agents/ and the main agent learns when to delegate.

Each file defines expertise, available tools, and handoff triggers. The main agent routes tasks automatically. A code review request goes to the reviewer. A “check for vulnerabilities” goes to the auditor.

You get specialization without manual routing.

6. Security Architecture: Prompt Injection Resistance

Section titled “6. Security Architecture: Prompt Injection Resistance”

Claude 4.5 includes improved defenses against prompt injection attacks. Testing shows the success rate dropped from 23.6% to 11.2%.

That’s not zero. Don’t blindly trust user input. But it means the model catches more injection attempts before they execute.

Layer your defenses: PreToolUse hooks for high-risk operations, output filtering for sensitive data, and rate limiting for external API calls.

Boris Cherny’s Power-User Patterns

Section titled “Boris Cherny’s Power-User Patterns”

Boris Cherny (author of Programming TypeScript) shared his workflow for getting more out of Claude:

Run 3-5 git worktrees in parallel. Each worktree gets its own Claude session. You can work on multiple features simultaneously without context switching. The sessions stay isolated.

Start complex tasks with plan mode. Don’t let the agent start coding immediately. Ask for a plan first. Review it. Then execute. You catch bad approaches before wasting time.

Update CLAUDE.md after every correction. When you fix a mistake, add a note to CLAUDE.md explaining what went wrong and the correct approach. Future sessions learn from past sessions.

Turn repeated tasks into skills. If you’ve explained something three times, write it as a skill. The skill file becomes reusable across projects.

Use subagents to keep main context clean. Long-running tasks accumulate context. Spawn subagents for focused work, let them finish, then summarize results back to main. Your primary session stays lean.

What This Means in Practice

Section titled “What This Means in Practice”

These aren’t theoretical features. They’re solutions to real problems:

  • Lifecycle hooks → Your agent won’t accidentally rm -rf /
  • Hot-reload → You can fix bugs without losing a 2-hour context window
  • Teleportation → Your agent follows you across machines
  • Dynamic MCP → You stop burning tokens on unused tools
  • Custom agents → Specialists handle specialized work
  • Better security → Fewer injection attacks succeed

The SDK gives you the primitives. How you combine them depends on what you’re building.

Section titled “Further Reading”
  • Claude Agent SDK Documentation
  • Nick Spisak’s original thread: @NickSpisak_
  • Boris Cherny’s tips: @bcherny

What patterns are you finding useful? Hit me up—always looking for new tricks.

Tessl: Giving Coding Agents the Context They Need to Succeed

Jan 25, 2026
Vibe Sparking

Introduction

Section titled “Introduction”

If you’ve used coding agents in real projects, you know the pattern. They get 80% of the way there, then stumble on API specifics—using deprecated methods, inventing parameters that don’t exist, or making assumptions that break in production. The code compiles, but it’s wrong.

Tessl is addressing this problem head-on with a deceptively simple idea: give agents structured, versioned context about the libraries they’re using. The results are compelling—up to 3.3x improvement in correct API usage across 300+ open-source packages.

The Problem: API Misuse

Section titled “The Problem: API Misuse”

Agents fail in predictable ways. When an LLM encounters a library it doesn’t know well (or knows an outdated version of), it doesn’t admit ignorance—it guesses. This creates brittle code that:

  • Uses non-existent or deprecated APIs
  • Ignores established patterns and idioms
  • Requires multiple rounds of fixes
  • Breaks when dependencies update

Tessl calls this “abstraction adherence”—whether an agent uses a library’s intended public interfaces instead of improvising. It’s a metric that matters far more than whether code simply compiles.

How Tessl Works

Section titled “How Tessl Works”

Tessl provides “tiles”—structured, versioned documentation specifically designed for AI agents to consume. Each tile covers a specific library and includes:

  • Correct API usage patterns
  • Version-specific information
  • Idiomatic examples
  • Common pitfalls

The key innovation is that tiles integrate directly into your project as dependencies. When you run tessl sync in your project, Tessl automatically:

  1. Scans your package.json or requirements.txt
  2. Matches dependencies to available tiles
  3. Ensures tiles match your installed versions
  4. Makes this context available via MCP to any agent

The Results

Section titled “The Results”

Across 300+ open-source packages on npm and PyPI, Tessl tiles demonstrated:

  • Up to 3.3x improvement in abstraction adherence for poorly-known packages
  • 1.2x improvement overall
  • 35% fewer integration errors
  • 1.4x faster completion on API-heavy tasks

The biggest gains come from libraries that agents typically struggle with—niche packages, newer versions, or specialized use cases not well-represented in training data.

Registry and Evals

Section titled “Registry and Evals”

Tessl maintains a public registry of tiles covering thousands of open-source libraries. What’s unique is that each tile includes published evals—you can see exactly how well agents perform with that specific library.

This transparency serves two purposes:

  1. Teams can track impact over time as models improve
  2. Library authors can contribute authoritative tiles for their projects

The registry is free to explore and integrates with major agent platforms via MCP.

Spec-Driven Development

Section titled “Spec-Driven Development”

Beyond library tiles, Tessl enables teams to encode their own conventions:

  • Directory layout rules
  • Naming conventions
  • Code style preferences
  • Architecture patterns

This means every AI contribution follows team standards without manual enforcement.

Industry Perspective

Section titled “Industry Perspective”

The platform has garnered attention from industry leaders:

“Spec-Driven Development is the next frontier in AI coding.” — Olivier Pomel, CEO, DataDog

“Tessl is the perfect antidote to vibe coding.” — Martin Wimpress, Sr Software Engineer, Chainguard

“There’s a big gap between demo-ware and production-ware.” — Des Traynor, Co-Founder, Intercom

The consensus is that structure and discipline—exactly what Tessl provides—are missing ingredients for reliable AI-assisted development.

Getting Started

Section titled “Getting Started”

Tessl offers a free tier to get started:

  1. Install the CLI: npm install -g @tessl/cli
  2. Run in your project: tessl sync
  3. Explore the registry at tessl.io/registry

The platform works with any agent supporting MCP, making it a flexible addition to existing AI workflows.

Looking Ahead

Section titled “Looking Ahead”

As AI agents become more embedded in development workflows (Gartner predicts 40% of enterprise apps will have task-specific agents by 2026), tools that provide reliable context will be critical.

Tessl’s approach—structured, versioned, eval-backed context—offers a path toward agents that don’t just write code, but write correct, maintainable code that follows team standards.

Claude Code + iMessage: The Complete Cure for Message Procrastination

Jan 19, 2026
Vibe Sparking

Introduction

Section titled “Introduction”

I have, historically, been embarrassingly bad at answering messages.

I either respond in 1 minute or 1 month. No in between.

A friend sends a text. I read it. I think “I should respond to this thoughtfully.” I put my phone down. Three weeks pass. Now it’s weird to respond. So I don’t. The relationship quietly erodes.

A client sends an email with a question. I know exactly what I need to say, but crafting the professional response feels like work. I’ll do it after I grab my coffee. Suddenly it’s the end of the day and my client has gone all day without a response.

This pattern has cost me more than I’d like to admit. Friendships that faded. Opportunities that disappeared. The guilt of unanswered messages piling up. The anxiety of opening my inbox.

I fixed this with Claude Code.

Yes, I know how that sounds. But hear me out.

Why This Isn’t Pathetic

Section titled “Why This Isn’t Pathetic”

Using AI to help respond to text messages sounds deeply unhinged. Like I’m some kind of antisocial robot who can’t handle basic human interaction.

That’s not what this is.

The problem isn’t a personality defect. It’s a quirk of how brains work. Once you understand it, using tools to work around it stops feeling pathetic and starts feeling like good strategy.

Why We Procrastinate on Replies

Section titled “Why We Procrastinate on Replies”
Psychological MechanismExplanation
Decision fatigueEvery message requires micro-decisions: What’s the right tone? How formal should I be? Should I apologize for the delay? Each decision depletes the same mental resource
Blank page problemWhen you can say anything, deciding what to say becomes overwhelming. Infinite possibilities create paralysis
Loss aversionWe’re wired to fear losses more than we value gains. Saying the wrong thing feels riskier than saying nothing. So we default to nothing
Working memory limitationsComposing a response requires holding multiple things in mind simultaneously: relationship context, message content, intended meaning, interpretation, word choice, tone. Human working memory caps around 4 items
Zeigarnik effectUnfinished tasks occupy mental space. Every unanswered message becomes a small cognitive burden

The Core Insight

Section titled “The Core Insight”

Reacting to a draft is dramatically easier than creating from scratch.

When someone shows you a paragraph and asks “does this sound right?”, you can immediately spot what’s off. But staring at a blank page trying to write that same paragraph? Torture.

Editing uses recognition. Creating uses recall. Recognition is fast and easy. Recall is slow and exhausting.

Claude gives you a draft to react to. You go from “what do I even say?” to “let me tweak this.”

Setting Up Claude Code on Mac

Section titled “Setting Up Claude Code on Mac”

On Mac, Claude Code can read your iMessages directly. Messages are stored locally in a SQLite database on your computer—Claude can query it without screenshots or copy-pasting.

Basic Usage

Section titled “Basic Usage”

Claude pulls the conversation. Then:

No screenshots. No switching apps. No friction.

What if You’re Not on Mac?

Section titled “What if You’re Not on Mac?”

Paste the message text directly, or drag in a screenshot—Claude can see images too.

The Context Advantage: MCPs

Section titled “The Context Advantage: MCPs”

Here’s where Claude Code pulls ahead of any other AI writing tool.

Claude Code can connect to external data sources through MCP (Model Context Protocol). This means when drafting a message, Claude isn’t working in a vacuum—it can pull in context from your actual life.

Someone asks “Are you free for lunch next week?”Calendar MCPClaude checks your real availability and drafts with specific times

Friend mentions something you talked about months agoSearch historyClaude searches conversation history and picks up the thread naturally

Common MCP Connections

  • Calendar — Know your real availability when scheduling
  • Email — Understand ongoing threads and context
  • Notes apps — Reference your own thinking and project details
  • CRM — Pull client history for professional responses

The difference is profound. Without MCPs, you’re asking Claude to draft a response to a message in isolation. With MCPs, Claude understands the full context—your schedule, your history with this person, your current projects, your notes—and drafts accordingly.

You stop providing context manually. Claude just knows.

Seven Real-World Patterns

Section titled “Seven Real-World Patterns”

Pattern 1: The Message You’ve Been Avoiding

Section titled “Pattern 1: The Message You’ve Been Avoiding”

You know the one. A friend reached out weeks ago. You meant to respond. Now it’s awkward.

“I’m the worst—just seeing this. Yes, let’s do it. Thursday or Friday work? I’ll come to you.”

90% of the message came from Claude. I tweaked two phrases. Total time: 30 seconds instead of three weeks of avoidance.

Pushing back on your boss. Giving critical feedback. Declining a request from a colleague who guilts you. These messages get postponed precisely because they’re hard.

Claude gives you the hard thing said in a way that isn’t confrontational. You read it, feel relieved, adjust for your specific dynamics, and send.

With calendar MCP:

Claude checks your real availability and drafts accordingly. No more manually cross-referencing your calendar, no more accidentally double-booking.

This is the lowest-stakes use case, but it adds up the most. These small messages take 30 seconds to write, but the friction of context-switching means they sit for hours.

Pattern 7: The Message You’re Dreading

Sometimes you need to say something genuinely difficult. Declining a wedding invitation. Breaking bad news. Ending a professional relationship. Setting a boundary with family.

The situation: You can’t afford to attend a friend’s destination wedding.

Your prompt:

The message that would have taken weeks to compose takes ten minutes. The relationship survives because you responded instead of avoiding.

Batch Processing Your Backlog

Here’s where this becomes transformative.

In 20 minutes, you clear weeks of communication debt.

The Proactive System: Beyond Responding

Section titled “The Proactive System: Beyond Responding”

Everything above is reactive. Someone messages you, you respond.

The other half of the problem: relationships fade because no one reaches out at all. You think about someone, mean to text them, don’t, and six months later you’ve drifted apart. Not from conflict—from entropy.

The Weekly Relationship Review

Section titled “The Weekly Relationship Review”

Every Sunday, before clearing your backlog:

Your prompt:

Section titled “The “Just Because” Message”

The hardest messages to send are the ones with no agenda.

Your prompt:

Claude’s draft:

“Random thought—saw someone at the coffee shop reading that book you recommended and it made me smile. Hope you’re doing well.”

That message takes two seconds to send. Without the draft, I’d overthink it for an hour and never send it.

The Life Events Tracker

Section titled “The Life Events Tracker”

People tell you things. Their kid is starting school. They’re training for a marathon. They just moved. You forget.

With a notes MCP connected, Claude can help you track these:

Then monthly:

“How did your daughter’s first week of school go?” lands completely differently than generic check-ins.

Voice Calibration

Section titled “Voice Calibration”

Claude doesn’t know how you talk. But you can teach it.

Option 1: Show Examples

Section titled “Option 1: Show Examples”

Option 2: Describe Your Style

Section titled “Option 2: Describe Your Style”

Option 3: Iterate

Section titled “Option 3: Iterate”

After a few rounds, you’ll internalize what directions produce your voice.

What NOT to Do

Section titled “What NOT to Do”
  • Don’t auto-send anything. Claude drafts. You review. You send. The human judgment step isn’t optional.
  • Don’t use this for high-stakes emotional conversations. Breaking up with someone? Working through conflict with a family member? Have the actual conversation.
  • Don’t use it to be someone you’re not. If Claude’s draft sounds more articulate than you’d ever be, people will notice. Edit toward authenticity, not perfection.
  • Don’t over-explain. “Sorry this took so long, I had Claude help me draft this” is weird. Just send the message.

Limitations

Section titled “Limitations”
LimitationDescription
Nuanced relationshipsClaude doesn’t know your history. It can’t know that “sounds good” from your sister actually means she’s upset
Office politicsClaude doesn’t know that your “suggestion” to your boss needs to be framed differently than to your direct report
Cultural normsWhat’s friendly in one culture is overly casual in another. Claude defaults to American professional-casual
Platform constraintsClaude doesn’t know LinkedIn messages should be shorter than emails, or that paragraphs over Instagram DM seem intense
Truly difficult emotional situationsAI can help you find words. It can’t replace emotional intelligence

The Deeper Point

Section titled “The Deeper Point”

The goal isn’t to optimize communication. It’s to actually communicate.

The messages I avoided weren’t unimportant. They were from friends I cared about, clients I valued, colleagues I respected. The avoidance wasn’t laziness—it was friction accumulating until the activation energy felt insurmountable.

Claude addresses this by turning “I need to figure out what to say” into “I need to react to this draft.”

Since I started doing this:

  • Average response time dropped dramatically
  • The guilt backlog is gone
  • Relationships that were fading are active again
  • I enjoy messaging instead of dreading it
  • I’m proactively maintaining relationships I used to let drift

The tool isn’t the point. The relationships are. The tool just removes what was getting in the way.

  2. Ask it to find your oldest unanswered iMessage:
  1. Draft a response:
  1. Review the draft
  2. Edit to your voice
  3. Send

One message. Today. Feel the relief.

The power-upMCPs let Claude pull context from your calendar, email, notes, and other tools

The workflow (other platforms)1. Paste or screenshot the message 2. Tell Claude: context, tone, key point 3. Get draft 4. Edit for your voice 5. Send

Don’t use it for:

Proactive system:

Introduction

Section titled “Introduction”

Game development is a complex, iterative process filled with repetitive tasks. Writing boilerplate code, setting up scenes, debugging scripts—these activities consume valuable time that could be spent on creative work.

Coplay is an AI assistant designed specifically for Unity game developers that lives directly inside the Unity Editor. Unlike generic AI coding tools, Coplay understands Unity’s architecture, components, and workflows deeply.

Why Coplay for Unity Development?

Section titled “Why Coplay for Unity Development?”

The Challenge of Traditional AI Tools

Section titled “The Challenge of Traditional AI Tools”

Most AI coding assistants operate at the code editor level, missing crucial context about your Unity project:

LimitationImpact
No Unity Editor awarenessCan’t manipulate scenes, prefabs, or game objects directly
Generic C# suggestionsDoesn’t understand Unity-specific patterns like coroutines, scriptable objects
Context switchingConstantly switching between IDE and browser for AI assistance

Coplay’s Unity-Native Advantage

Section titled “Coplay’s Unity-Native Advantage”

Coplay integrates as a C# plugin directly into Unity Editor, giving it:

  • Direct Scene Access: Manipulate GameObjects, components, and hierarchies
  • Unity Pattern Recognition: Understands MonoBehaviours, ScriptableObjects, serialization
  • Asset Pipeline Integration: Can work with prefabs, materials, and assets
  • Natural Language Interface: Describe what you want in plain English

Prerequisites

Section titled “Prerequisites”
  • Unity 2022.3 or newer (LTS recommended)
  • Coplay supports both Unity Personal and Professional licenses

Installation Steps

Section titled “Installation Steps”

  1. Open Unity Package Manager

    • Window > Package Manager
    • Click the + icon
    • Select “Add package from git URL”

  2. Install Coplay Plugin

  3. Configure API Key

    • Open Edit > Preferences > Coplay
    • Enter your API key (sign up at coplay.dev)

Quick Start Workflow

Section titled “Quick Start Workflow”
  1. Open Coplay Panel: Window > Coplay
  2. Describe Your Task: “Create a player movement script with WASD controls”
  3. Review Suggestions: Coplay shows code you can preview
  4. Apply Changes: One-click to insert into your project

Core Features

1. Code Generation

Section titled “1. Code Generation”

Generate Unity-specific scripts with proper patterns:

2. Scene Manipulation

CommandAction
”Find all GameObjects with tag ‘Enemy‘“Returns filtered list
”Add a rigidbody to the player”Attaches component
”Create a cube at position (0, 2, 0)“Instantiates object
”Parent all coins to the coin manager”Reorganizes hierarchy

PlanPriceFeatures
Free$0Use your own API key, pay-as-you-go
ProfessionalFrom $29/moIncluded credits, priority support

See coplay.dev/pricing for current details.

Best Practices

Section titled “Best Practices”

1. Be Specific with Context

Section titled “1. Be Specific with Context”

Good: “Create a third-person camera controller that smooth-follows the player with adjustable distance and height, using Cinemachine if available”

Bad: “Make a camera script”

2. Iterate in Small Steps

Break complex features into manageable pieces:

  1. First: “Create basic player movement”
  2. Then: “Add jumping with gravity”
  3. Then: “Add sprint mechanics”
  4. Finally: “Add camera follow”

Coplay represents a new category of AI tools: environment-aware assistants that understand the context of your specific development environment.

For Unity developers, Coplay isn’t just another coding assistant—it’s a collaborator that speaks your language, understands your tools, and helps you ship games faster.

Introduction

In the rapidly evolving landscape of AI-powered development tools, OpenCode has emerged as a formidable open-source alternative to commercial AI coding assistants. But if you’re a hacker who loves customization and maximum control, Oh My OpenCode is the plugin that transforms OpenCode into something extraordinary.

Created by developer code-yeongyu after spending $24,000 worth of tokens on personal development with various AI tools, Oh My OpenCode represents the distillation of countless hours of testing, configuration, and real-world usage. It’s described by its author as “OpenCode on steroids” — and for good reason.

“If Claude Code does in 7 days what a human does in 3 months, Sisyphus does it in 1 hour. It just works until the task is done. It is a disciplined agent.” — B, Quant Researcher

What is Oh My OpenCode?

Oh My OpenCode is a comprehensive plugin for OpenCode that adds:

  • Async Subagents — Run multiple AI agents in parallel, just like Claude Code
  • Curated Agents — Pre-configured specialist agents with optimal models
  • Crafted Tools — LSP and AST grep tools for powerful code manipulation
  • Curated MCPs — Built-in Model Context Protocol servers for extended capabilities
  • Claude Code Compatibility — Full compatibility layer for Claude Code configs

The plugin is battle-tested in production environments and has already helped developers accomplish remarkable feats:

At the heart of Oh My OpenCode is Sisyphus, the default orchestrator agent named after the Greek mythological figure condemned to roll a boulder up a hill for eternity.

“In greek mythology, Sisyphus was condemned to roll a boulder up a hill for eternity as punishment for deceiving the gods. LLM Agents haven’t really done anything wrong, yet they too roll their ‘stones’—their thoughts—every single day. My life is no different. Looking back, we are not so different from these agents.”

pg-aiguide: AI-Optimized PostgreSQL Expertise for Coding Assistants

Section titled “pg-aiguide: AI-Optimized PostgreSQL Expertise for Coding Assistants”

In the rapidly evolving landscape of AI-powered development tools, one challenge has persisted: AI coding assistants often generate database code that is outdated, missing critical constraints, unaware of modern PostgreSQL features, and inconsistent with real-world best practices.

Enter pg-aiguide – an innovative MCP server and Claude plugin developed by Timescale (now Tiger Data) that provides AI-optimized PostgreSQL expertise to coding assistants.

What is pg-aiguide?

Section titled “What is pg-aiguide?”

pg-aiguide is an open-source tool (Apache-2.0 licensed) that helps AI coding tools write dramatically better PostgreSQL code. It provides three core capabilities:

  1. Semantic Search across the official PostgreSQL manual (version-aware)
  2. AI-Optimized Skills – curated, opinionated Postgres best practices used automatically by AI agents
  3. Extension Ecosystem Docs, starting with TimescaleDB, with more extensions coming soon

The Problem pg-aiguide Solves

Section titled “The Problem pg-aiguide Solves”

AI coding tools frequently generate PostgreSQL code that suffers from several issues:

  • Outdated syntax – not keeping up with modern PostgreSQL versions
  • Missing constraints and indexes – leading to poor data integrity and performance
  • Unaware of modern PG features – missing out on capabilities introduced in recent versions
  • Inconsistent with best practices – not following proven patterns from experienced developers

Real-World Impact

Section titled “Real-World Impact”

The pg-aiguide team conducted an impressive comparison test. When asked to create an e-commerce database schema:

  • 4× more constraints compared to AI without pg-aiguide
  • 55% more indexes (including partial and expression indexes)
  • PG17-recommended patterns – using the latest PostgreSQL features
  • Modern features like GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY and NULLS NOT DISTINCT
  • Cleaner naming & documentation – more maintainable code
